name: Ashwagandha
summary: A root traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine and now widely sold as an adaptogen supplement for stress, anxiety, and sleep, with a growing body of small-to-moderate randomized trials showing a consistent direction of benefit for those uses; its safety profile is meaningfully more serious than many other popular herbs, with a well-documented, occasionally severe liver-injury signal and a trial-confirmed effect on thyroid hormones that make it unsuitable for some people without medical guidance.

claims.useCase: Stress, anxiety, and elevated cortisol (oral root extract)
claims.gradeRationale: Multiple independent randomized trials point the same direction. Chandrasekhar et al. 2012 (n=64, KSM-66 extract 300mg twice daily, 60 days) found the Perceived Stress Scale fell 44.0% with ashwagandha versus 5.5% with placebo (P<0.0001), with serum cortisol falling 27.9% versus 7.9% (P=0.002) — though the tested extract was manufacturer-supplied by Ixoreal Biomed despite the paper declaring no conflict of interest, worth weighing when reading this as an independent result. Fuladi et al. 2021 tested a clinical population with confirmed DSM-IV-TR Generalized Anxiety Disorder (n=40 adults, 1g/day as an SSRI add-on, 6 weeks) and found HAM-A scores fell 14 points versus 8 with placebo (P<0.05). A peer-reviewed meta-analysis (Akhgarjand et al. 2022, 12 RCTs, 1,002 participants) found a significant pooled effect on anxiety (SMD -1.55) and stress (SMD -1.75), but its own authors rate 'the certainty of the evidence was low for both outcomes' with very high heterogeneity (I²=83-94%); a 2025 conference-abstract meta-analysis (15 studies, 873 patients, not yet full peer-reviewed) reports similarly consistent findings on HAM-A, PSS, and cortisol. NCCIH's own framing is narrower than the trial literature: 'some ashwagandha preparations may be effective for insomnia and stress' but 'evidence is unclear about its effects on anxiety.' Graded C: a consistent positive direction across genuinely independent research groups, including one trial in confirmed-GAD patients, but the peer-reviewed meta-analysis's own authors call certainty low, heterogeneity is very high, the largest single trial used manufacturer-supplied extract, and several of the positive trials share overlapping authorship — not independent replications of each other in the fullest sense.

claims.useCase: Sleep quality, including in people with confirmed insomnia (oral root extract)
claims.gradeRationale: Langade et al. 2019 (n=60, 300mg full-spectrum root extract twice daily, 10 weeks, with objective actigraphy plus PSQI and HAM-A) found sleep onset latency improved to 29.00 minutes versus 33.94 minutes with placebo at week 10 (p=0.019), sleep efficiency rose from 75.63% to 83.48% versus a smaller placebo-group rise, and subjective sleep quality improved significantly (p=0.002), with no competing interests reported by the authors. An independent systematic review and meta-analysis (Cheah et al. 2021, 5 RCTs, 400 participants total) found a small but significant overall effect (SMD -0.59, I²=62%), with the benefit 'more prominent' in a subgroup with confirmed insomnia taking at least 600mg/day for at least 8 weeks; the same review found improved morning alertness and 'no serious side effects' in the pooled trials, while cautioning that data on serious adverse effects remain limited. Graded C: a consistent small-to-moderate positive effect across an independent systematic review, concentrated in a confirmed-insomnia, higher-dose subgroup, but with only moderate trial count and the reviewers' own caution about limited long-term safety data.

claims.useCase: Athletic performance and strength gains in resistance training (oral root extract)
claims.gradeRationale: One detailed randomized trial (Wankhede et al. 2015, n=57 resistance-trained men, 300mg twice daily, 8 weeks) found significantly greater gains in bench press and leg extension one-rep max, muscle cross-sectional area, and testosterone (+96.2 ng/dL versus +18.0 ng/dL with placebo, p=0.004) compared with placebo. However, this trial was not independently replicated by a different research group or extract brand within this research, its funding/conflict-of-interest disclosure could not be confirmed from the retrievable abstract, and it shares an author with other ashwagandha-positive trials in this entry — a pattern worth noting rather than treating each trial as a fully independent replication of the others. NCCIH lists athletic performance only among uses ashwagandha is 'promoted for,' without a separate evidence statement, implying the agency does not consider this use adequately established. Left ungraded pending independent replication, per this project's convention for single-trial, unreplicated findings.

claims.useCase: Male fertility and testosterone in men with low sperm count (oligospermia)
claims.gradeRationale: One self-labeled pilot trial (Ambiye et al. 2013, n=46 oligospermic men with sperm count under 20 million/mL, 675mg/day divided across three doses, 90 days) found sperm count rose from 9.59 to 25.61 million/mL, a 167% increase (P<0.0001), with semen volume and motility also improving significantly versus a placebo group described only as showing 'minimal' improvement; the abstract reports improved hormone levels generally but gives no specific testosterone figure. NCCIH corroborates the direction but with notably more caution, stating 'taking ashwagandha for 2 to 4 months may increase testosterone levels and sperm quality' — phrased as 'may,' consistent with limited rather than settled evidence. This is a single, explicitly self-labeled pilot trial with no independent replication found in this specific population, so it is left ungraded pending a larger confirmatory trial.

claims.useCase: Subclinical hypothyroidism (thyroid-hormone normalization)
claims.gradeRationale: A single small pilot trial (Sharma et al. 2018, n=50 adults with subclinical hypothyroidism, TSH 4.5-10 uIU/L, 600mg/day, 8 weeks) found a significant between-group effect on TSH (p<0.001), T3 (p=0.0031), and T4 (p=0.0096) favoring ashwagandha, with the authors framing this as ashwagandha 'may be beneficial for normalizing thyroid indices in subclinical hypothyroid patients.' This same trial-confirmed ability to raise T3/T4 and lower TSH is exactly what makes ashwagandha a safety concern for people who are hyperthyroid or on thyroid medication — see the thyroid safety note below, which should be read alongside this claim. A single small pilot trial is not enough evidence for a positive-use grade on its own, especially given the same mechanism carries real risk in the opposite direction; left ungraded and framed narrowly to subclinical hypothyroidism specifically, not as a general thyroid-support claim.

safetyNotes.text: Ashwagandha carries a well-documented, occasionally severe liver-injury signal. NIH's LiverTox database gives it a Likelihood Score of B — a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury — cataloging 14 individually documented case reports from 2017-2024 across 8 countries. Most cases were mild-to-moderate and self-limited, resolving within 1 to 4 months of stopping the product, but fatal cases from acute liver failure have been described, particularly in people with pre-existing liver disease or cirrhosis; one documented case progressed to hepatic encephalopathy requiring emergency liver transplantation. LiverTox specifically notes that in several reported cases the product was tested and found to be pure ashwagandha, not an adulterated or contaminated product. MSKCC independently corroborates with its own list of serious case-report categories, and NCCIH separately acknowledges cases linking liver injury to ashwagandha and states there isn't enough information to draw conclusions about its long-term safety. Anyone with liver disease or cirrhosis should avoid ashwagandha, and anyone taking it who develops jaundice, dark urine, or persistent abdominal pain should stop use and seek care.

Ashwagandha has a trial-confirmed ability to raise T3 and T4 and lower TSH (see the subclinical hypothyroidism claim above), which makes it a real concern — not merely theoretical — for people with hyperthyroidism, Graves' disease, or who take thyroid hormone medication. NCCIH advises against use for those with thyroid disorders and names thyroid hormone medications specifically as an interaction category; RxList rates the thyroid-hormone-medication interaction Minor but describes a risk of too much thyroid hormone in the body; MSKCC independently reports multiple case reports of thyrotoxicosis linked to ashwagandha use. Anyone with a thyroid condition or on thyroid medication should talk with a healthcare provider before use.

Ashwagandha should be avoided during pregnancy. NCCIH, RxList, and MSKCC all independently advise against use in pregnancy, with RxList rating it 'likely unsafe' and citing a risk of miscarriage; NCCIH also advises against use while breastfeeding. None of these sources detail the underlying mechanism, but the contraindication itself is corroborated by three independent reputable sources.

Ashwagandha may add to the effect of sedatives and other CNS depressants, including benzodiazepines and barbiturates. NCCIH, RxList (which rates both benzodiazepines and general CNS depressants a Moderate interaction), and MSKCC all independently name this interaction. Anyone taking sedating medication should use caution and talk with a healthcare provider.
NCCIH names anti-seizure (anticonvulsant) medications directly as an interaction category for ashwagandha. Anyone taking anticonvulsant medication should talk with a healthcare provider before use.

Ashwagandha may decrease the effectiveness of immunosuppressant medications. RxList rates this a Moderate interaction, NCCIH names immunosuppressants directly in its interaction guidance and separately advises against use for autoimmune disorders generally, and MSKCC reports a real documented case of kidney transplant rejection linked to ashwagandha use. Given that case-report weight, anyone taking immunosuppressant medication (including organ-transplant recipients) should avoid ashwagandha or use only under close medical supervision.

Ashwagandha may lower blood sugar and blood pressure, which can add to the effect of diabetes medications or antihypertensive medications and increase the risk of levels going too low. RxList rates both interactions Moderate, and NCCIH corroborates generally for diabetes and blood-pressure medications. Anyone on these medications should monitor closely and talk with a healthcare provider before combining them with ashwagandha.

NCCIH advises against use for people about to have surgery, and RxList recommends stopping ashwagandha at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery, likely related to its sedative, blood-sugar, and blood-pressure effects noted above.

Because ashwagandha has shown a testosterone-raising effect in clinical trials (see athletic performance and male fertility claims above), NCCIH and MSKCC both advise that people with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer should avoid its use.

NCCIH describes short-term use (up to about 3 months) as possibly safe, with common side effects including drowsiness, stomach upset, diarrhea, and vomiting, but states there isn't enough information to draw conclusions about long-term safety. This general tolerability profile should not be read as contradicting the liver-injury case-report signal above, since case reports by definition involve people whose use was not uneventful.

No WHO, German Commission E, or EU (EMA/HMPC) herbal monograph exists for ashwagandha, so there is no officially recognized effective dose. HMPC's 2013 public statement concluded a Community herbal monograph could not be established due to insufficient data. Poland's national health authority (Resolution 7/2020) went further and set a regulatory intake ceiling — no more than 3 g of powdered root and no more than 10 mg of withanolides per day — after a Danish DTU safety review concluded no dose could be established as unambiguously safe.

Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration requires a specific caution statement on ashwagandha products exceeding 12 g per day of equivalent dry root (for water-, ethanol-, or methanol-based extracts), a threshold informed by a rat reproductive and developmental toxicology study (Prabu & Panchapakesan, 2015). As with the Polish limit above, this is a regulatory safety ceiling, not a recommended effective dose.

name: Astragalus
summary: A root native to northern and eastern China, Mongolia, and Korea, central to Traditional Chinese Medicine as a qi (vital-energy) tonic traditionally taken to build resistance to illness and fatigue. Modern research on astragalus is almost entirely made up of small Chinese trials that add it to standard care rather than testing it alone, and shows a repeatedly observed direction of benefit for immune-marker changes, as an adjunct alongside metformin for type 2 diabetes, as an adjunct alongside standard therapy for kidney disease, and for easing cancer-related fatigue during chemotherapy. Every systematic review located rates the underlying trial quality as low, and NCCIH's own conclusion is that there isn't yet sufficient reliable evidence that astragalus is useful for any specific health condition.

claims.useCase: Immune function support (immune-marker changes)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH cites a 2023 review of 19 studies (1,094 participants) finding astragalus lowered several proinflammatory cytokines and shifted immune-cell ratios, but describes the underlying studies as small and inconsistently designed. That review (Zhang et al., 2023) reports large effect sizes, but its participant count matches NCCIH's own citation exactly, so this is not independently corroborated by a second source, and the outcomes measured are lab markers rather than clinical results like fewer infections. Left ungraded given the single-review-family sourcing and the gap between marker changes and confirmed clinical benefit.

citations.label: NCCIH: Astragalus
Zhang et al., "The Effect of Astragalus on Humoral and Cellular Immune Response: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Human Studies" (Complementary Medicine Research, 2023)

claims.useCase: Adjunct alongside metformin for type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose, HbA1c)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH cites a 2024 review of 20 studies (953 adults with type 2 diabetes) finding astragalus added to metformin lowered fasting blood glucose and HbA1c more than metformin alone. That review's own authors describe most included trials as low quality with meaningful risk of bias, and its participant count again matches NCCIH's citation exactly rather than an independently found second source. Every trial compared astragalus-plus-metformin to metformin alone - none tested astragalus by itself against a placebo. Left ungraded given the authors' own quality caveats and the single-review-family sourcing.

"The Efficacy and Safety of Astragalus as an Adjuvant Treatment for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis" (Journal of Integrative and Complementary Medicine, 2024)

claims.useCase: Adjunct alongside standard therapy for idiopathic membranous nephropathy (proteinuria, kidney-function markers)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH cites a 2023 review of 50 studies (3,423 participants, all conducted in China) finding astragalus added to standard nephropathy therapy improved some kidney-health indicators versus that therapy alone. The underlying review reports very high statistical heterogeneity across its outcomes (I-squared 91-94%) and its own authors caution that the overall evidence quality is low. As with the immune and diabetes claims above, this traces to the same single review NCCIH itself cites, not an independently found second source. Left ungraded given the heterogeneity and quality caveats.

claims.useCase: Easing cancer-related fatigue as a chemotherapy adjunct
claims.gradeRationale: A dedicated 2025 review of 8 randomized trials (804 participants) found astragalus reduced fatigue and improved quality of life during chemotherapy, and MSKCC separately lists cancer-related fatigue reduction among astragalus's studied uses - genuine, independent double-sourcing, unlike the claims above. However, both sources rate the evidence quality as low to very low, and the trials studied were overwhelmingly IV astragalus polysaccharide injections or acupoint injections rather than the oral tea, capsule, or tincture forms this glossary otherwise covers - a meaningful mismatch in how the herb was actually administered. Left ungraded given the low trial quality and the oral-vs-injectable administration gap.

safetyNotes.text: NCCIH states astragalus may be safe when taken orally, and that doses up to 60 grams per day for as long as 4 months have not been shown to cause adverse effects - but a thorough safety evaluation has not been done, and there isn't enough reliable information to know whether applying astragalus to the skin is safe.
NCCIH advises people with autoimmune diseases avoid astragalus, since it may worsen autoimmune symptoms - consistent with astragalus's own immune-stimulating effects described above.

NCCIH and MSKCC both independently document that astragalus may interact with immunosuppressant medications. MSKCC cites a specific case report of astragalus reducing blood levels of the transplant drug tacrolimus by nearly half, a serious risk for anyone on immunosuppressant therapy after an organ transplant or for an autoimmune condition.

MSKCC states astragalus has anticoagulant properties and may increase bleeding risk; this was not independently found in NCCIH's own content, so treat it as a single-sourced but clinically meaningful caution, particularly for anyone taking blood thinners or antiplatelet medication.

MSKCC separately documents possible interactions with diuretics (astragalus has a natriuretic effect that could be additive), antihypertensive medications (astragalus extract has been shown to lower blood pressure, raising a risk of additive hypotension), hormonal therapies (astragalus has estrogenic properties that may interfere), and chemotherapy drugs that are substrates of the P-glycoprotein transporter, since astragalus polysaccharides may increase their cytotoxicity - relevant to anyone considering astragalus alongside chemotherapy for the fatigue-related use above. Talk with a doctor or pharmacist before combining astragalus with any of these.
MSKCC lists fatigue, malaise, headache, and lowered blood pressure as reported adverse effects of astragalus use.
NCCIH states little is known about whether astragalus is safe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and that animal research suggests it can be toxic to a developing fetus during pregnancy.

As with other herbal dietary supplements, astragalus products are not tested or approved by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale, so actual content can vary between products and may not match label claims.

name: Black Cohosh
summary: A tall North American woodland plant whose dried root and rhizome are used in dietary supplements, most studied today for easing menopausal hot flashes and other vasomotor symptoms, though trial results have been genuinely inconsistent; it also carries a well-documented, though rare, risk of serious liver injury.

claims.useCase: Menopausal hot flashes and other vasomotor symptoms (oral black cohosh root/rhizome extract, e.g. Remifemin-brand products)
claims.gradeRationale: Evidence across black cohosh trials for menopausal hot flashes is genuinely inconsistent rather than clearly positive. NCCIH states research on black cohosh products has had inconsistent results and that an earlier 2012 review concluded there was not enough evidence to support its use for menopause symptoms; a 2015 North American Menopause Society position statement, while not black-cohosh-specific, recommended hypnotherapy for hot flashes but did not recommend acupuncture, yoga, or any natural products (a category that includes black cohosh). NCCIH also cites a 2023 review of 22 studies finding black cohosh products potentially beneficial for overall menopause symptoms, with improvement specifically in hot flashes but not in anxiety or depressive symptoms. An independent secondary summary (Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center) similarly describes the data as conflicting, noting an older meta-analysis found insufficient evidence while a more recent meta-analysis found an isopropanolic black cohosh extract comparable to low-dose transdermal estradiol for symptom relief. Left ungraded given more than a decade of genuinely mixed trial- and review-level conclusions, product-to-product variability, and NCCIH's own current framing that overall usefulness for menopause symptoms remains unsettled.

citations.label: NCCIH: Black Cohosh
NCCIH: Menopausal Symptoms: In Depth
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center: Black Cohosh

claims.useCase: Traditional/historical use for menstrual discomfort and other complaints (menstrual cramps, premenstrual symptoms, and historically for sore throat, kidney complaints, and to help bring on labor)
claims.gradeRationale: Black cohosh has a long history of Native American use for kidney ailments, malaria, sore throat, and menstrual cramps, and has more recently been promoted for premenstrual symptoms and to help induce labor. NCCIH states there is not enough reliable data to show whether black cohosh is effective for any of these other uses beyond the limited hot-flash research above. Left ungraded: this reflects traditional and historical use only, without a clinical evidence base of its own, and using black cohosh to attempt to bring on labor is specifically discouraged given the lack of safety data (see safety notes).

citations.label: NCCIH: Black Cohosh

safetyNotes.text: Black cohosh carries a well-documented, though rare, risk of serious liver injury. NIH's LiverTox database gives black cohosh a Likelihood Score of A - a well-established cause of clinically apparent liver injury - with reported cases ranging from moderate liver-enzyme elevations to acute liver failure that has required liver transplantation or resulted in death; onset is usually 2 to 12 weeks after starting use (reported range about 1 to 48 weeks). The injury appears to be an idiosyncratic, possibly immune-mediated reaction rather than a predictable dose-dependent effect, and LiverTox notes that unknown adulterants or products mislabeled as black cohosh (DNA testing has found some commercial products actually derived from other Actaea species) may account for some cases. Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration has required a liver-injury warning statement on black cohosh products sold there. NCCIH similarly reports rare but sometimes very serious cases of liver damage in people taking commercial black cohosh products, while noting that causality has not been proven in every case. Anyone with an existing liver disorder should talk to a healthcare provider before use, and anyone taking black cohosh who develops abdominal pain, dark urine, or jaundice should stop use and contact a healthcare provider promptly.

More commonly, black cohosh use has been associated with mild gastrointestinal upset, nausea, vomiting, rash, dizziness, and headache; NCCIH describes side effects overall as generally mild, if they occur at all.

It is uncertain whether black cohosh is safe for people with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast or uterine cancer, and NCCIH advises talking with a healthcare provider first. The underlying mechanism is debated: some laboratory research summarized by Memorial Sloan Kettering has found black cohosh extracts do not change LH, FSH, prolactin, or estradiol levels (arguing against a classic estrogenic effect), while separate laboratory research in mice reported an increased incidence of metastatic disease with black cohosh exposure. Given this unresolved uncertainty, people with a current or past hormone-sensitive cancer should discuss use with their oncologist before taking black cohosh.

Laboratory research summarized by Memorial Sloan Kettering describes black cohosh potentially interfering with the action of the breast-cancer drug tamoxifen (clinical relevance not established) and potentially increasing the toxicity of the chemotherapy drugs doxorubicin and docetaxel (clinical significance not yet determined). People undergoing these cancer therapies should not combine them with black cohosh without their oncologist's guidance.

A phytochemical analysis isolated several cycloartane triterpene glycosides from a commercial black cohosh supplement and found the supplement inhibited the CYP3A4 liver enzyme, which metabolizes a large share of prescription drugs; the study authors advised avoiding concomitant use of black cohosh with any CYP3A4-metabolized medication (the paper's own examples were cyclosporine, benzodiazepines, and calcium-channel blockers, not statins specifically). Given black cohosh's own documented liver-injury risk described above, anyone taking prescription medication metabolized by the liver should talk with a healthcare provider before adding black cohosh.

NCCIH states black cohosh may not be safe to use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and it should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding, including as a traditional preparation to attempt to bring on or strengthen labor, given this lack of safety data.

name: Chasteberry
summary: A berry from the chaste tree, traditionally used for menstrual and reproductive complaints and most studied today as an oral extract for premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and cyclical breast pain (mastalgia), where a real body of randomized-trial evidence exists but carries substantial heterogeneity and risk-of-bias concerns. Evidence for menopause symptoms and fertility/luteal-phase support is weaker and more mixed, and no dedicated trial evidence was found for acne, which instead appears as a listed side effect in the safety literature. Its core pharmacology — binding pituitary dopamine D2 receptors to alter prolactin secretion — is also the basis of its most safety-relevant feature: a real, though not fully quantified in clinical-trial terms, potential interaction with dopamine-related medications (antipsychotics, Parkinson's drugs) and with hormonal medications (birth control, HRT); it is generally advised against in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and hormone-sensitive conditions.

claims.useCase: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)
claims.gradeRationale: Three independent systematic reviews of randomized trials agree on the direction of benefit but diverge on how much to trust the magnitude. Cerqueira et al. (Arch Womens Ment Health, 2017) reviewed 8 RCTs across three different chasteberry preparations and found all eight positive, concluding it represents 'a safe and efficacious alternative to be considered.' Verkaik et al. (Am J Obstet Gynecol, 2017), the largest and most quantitatively rigorous review, pooled 14 RCTs and found a large effect on total PMS symptoms (Hedges' g -1.21, 95% CI -1.53 to -0.88), but explicitly cautioned that very high heterogeneity (I²=91%), high risk of bias in most included trials, and evidence of publication bias mean 'the treatment effect estimates likely overestimate the true efficacy.' van Die et al. (Planta Med, 2013) found most trials favored chasteberry over placebo for PMS specifically, but results against fluoxetine for PMDD were genuinely mixed (one trial found equivalence, another found fluoxetine more effective). Graded C: a real, repeatedly positive signal across three independent reviews with generally mild, infrequent adverse events, but the single most rigorous meta-analysis itself warns that its own pooled effect size likely overstates true efficacy — this should be presented as consistently positive in direction, not a settled large effect.

claims.useCase: Cyclical mastalgia (breast pain and tenderness)
claims.gradeRationale: Ooi, Watts, McClean & Pak (J Womens Health, 2020) reviewed 25 studies and pooled a stricter meta-analysis subset of 6 studies (718 participants) finding a moderate effect favoring chasteberry over placebo (SMD 0.67, 95% CI 0.5-0.85) at a typical dose of 20-40 mg/day over about 3 months. Seven trials in the review found chasteberry noninferior to standard comparators including dopamine agonists, NSAIDs, SSRIs/SNRIs, and hormonal contraceptives, consistent with a prolactin-lowering mechanism in this reproductive-age population. Most included studies were rated as having an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient reporting detail. NCCIH and MSKCC independently corroborate the general direction ('might reduce PMS symptoms such as breast pain or tenderness,' though NCCIH notes 'higher-quality evidence' is needed). Graded C: a moderate, reasonably precise pooled effect size with a real noninferiority signal against standard treatments, but resting on a single dedicated meta-analysis not independently corroborated by a second one, and with real reporting-quality limitations across the underlying trials.

claims.useCase: Menopause (climacteric) symptoms
claims.gradeRationale: This is genuinely conflicting evidence rather than a settled question. Laakmann et al. (Gynecol Endocrinol, 2012), a systematic review assessed by four independent reviewers, concluded chasteberry 'showed no better effect than placebo' for climacteric complaints, and that combining it with St. John's wort also showed no significant difference versus comparators. A more recent, smaller RCT — Naseri et al. (Korean J Fam Med, 2019), 52 participants analyzed after dropouts — found significant improvement on the anxiety, vasomotor, and total Greene Climacteric Scale scores, but no significant difference on the depression, somatic-complaint, or sexual-dysfunction subscales. NCCIH describes only 'a preliminary study' suggesting possible benefit; MSKCC states chasteberry helps PMS symptoms 'but not menopause symptoms,' and that a chasteberry plus St. John's wort combination 'was ineffective for treating menopausal symptoms.' Left ungraded: a systematic review's null finding versus a small, more recent single RCT's partial positive finding is real disagreement that should not be flattened into either a clear win or a clear failure; weight should lean toward the systematic review's null finding given its broader evidence base.

claims.useCase: Fertility support / luteal-phase support
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states directly that there isn't enough reliable evidence to confirm a benefit for infertility or related sexual-health concerns. The two trials located that address this use case both test multi-ingredient combination products (Fertilityblend and Phyto-Hypophyson L), not isolated chasteberry, so their findings — including a significant luteal-phase-temperature improvement and a higher pregnancy rate for Fertilityblend, and a significant composite-outcome benefit for Phyto-Hypophyson L specifically in women with oligomenorrhea — cannot be attributed to chasteberry alone. A separate, more directly relevant sub-finding comes from van Die et al.'s 2013 pooled review: of 12 trials reviewed, 2 addressed latent hyperprolactinemia (which can disrupt ovulation and fertility), finding chasteberry outperformed placebo in one trial and performed comparably to the prolactin-lowering drug bromocriptine in another. This is a plausible mechanistic pathway, not a direct fertility or live-birth outcome trial. Left ungraded: no dedicated, well-designed trial isolating chasteberry alone against a fertility or luteal-phase-length outcome was found.

claims.useCase: Acne
claims.gradeRationale: No dedicated trial testing chasteberry as an intervention for acne was found. Chasteberry appears in several PCOS-related reviews as one ingredient among several where acne is one of several PCOS symptoms, but none isolate an acne-specific outcome for chasteberry alone. Notably, a systematic review of chasteberry adverse events (Daniele, Thompson Coon, Pittler & Ernst, 2005) lists acne among the most commonly reported adverse effects of chasteberry use itself, alongside nausea, headache, gastrointestinal disturbances, menstrual disorders, pruritus, and erythematous rash — plausibly consistent with the herb's hormonal/prolactin-modulating mechanism, since androgenic/hormonal shifts are a known driver of acne. Left ungraded and flagged prominently: available evidence does not support chasteberry as an acne remedy, and acne instead appears in the literature as a possible side effect rather than a benefit.

safetyNotes.text: Chasteberry's dopaminergic compounds act on pituitary dopamine D2 receptors and dose-dependently alter prolactin release (low doses may increase it, high doses decrease it). Because of this mechanism, it should not be combined with dopamine-antagonist medications (antipsychotics) or dopamine-agonist medications (Parkinson's drugs) without a prescriber's guidance, as it may interfere with these drugs' action or enhance their side effects. This is corroborated across MSKCC, LactMed, and a systematic review of chasteberry adverse events, though all three describe it as a theoretical/mechanistic concern — actual reported clinical-outcome cases of harm are thin.

Chasteberry may decrease the effectiveness of hormonal medications, including birth control and hormone replacement therapy (HRT), per MSKCC and the NIH LiverTox monograph; the LiverTox monograph specifically advises against use in women on birth control or hormone replacement.

Chasteberry is generally advised against during pregnancy and breastfeeding, corroborated across four independent sources (NCCIH, MSKCC, LactMed, and a systematic review of adverse events). LactMed notes potential to decrease lactation at higher doses and cautions that no scientifically valid clinical trials support using it as a galactogogue; infant-level pharmacokinetic data was not found in the literature reviewed.

Chasteberry may not be safe for those with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine, or ovarian cancer (NCCIH); MSKCC similarly advises patients with hormone-sensitive cancers to consult their physician before use.

MSKCC states chasteberry inhibits CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and may affect drugs metabolized by these enzymes, based on preclinical data with clinical relevance not yet determined. This is currently a single-source claim not independently corroborated by NCCIH, LiverTox, or a pharmacokinetic study found during research — present as a plausible but unconfirmed metabolic-interaction caution.

Commonly reported mild adverse effects, corroborated across NCCIH, MSKCC, and a dedicated systematic review of adverse events: nausea, stomach pain or GI disturbances, headache, menstrual changes, and skin reactions including acne, itching, and rash. Generally described as mild and reversible.

Liver safety is reassuring and well-documented: NIH's LiverTox database assigns chasteberry Likelihood Category E (unlikely cause of clinically apparent liver injury), citing checks across the Swedish adverse-reaction registry, the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network, the Spanish and Latin American DILI registries, and a large systematic review of 936 herb-induced liver injury cases — none implicated chaste tree. One isolated case report of hepatitis exists, but LiverTox itself notes other possible causes were not adequately excluded, so causality was not established.

A single, unconfirmed spontaneous report of Stevens-Johnson syndrome associated with chaste tree use is noted in the LiverTox monograph's bibliography; causality was not established and this should not be presented as a demonstrated risk.

As a dietary supplement, chasteberry is not pre-approved by the FDA for safety or efficacy before sale. NCCIH notes it has been used safely in studies only for up to 3 months, so longer-term safety data is comparatively thin.

name: Echinacea
summary: A North American prairie plant traditionally used by Native Americans for respiratory infections and now widely sold as a supplement thought to lower the odds of catching a cold or shorten its course; a large, methodologically conservative Cochrane review found no significant effect on catching a cold in any single trial comparison while a more aggressively-pooled 2007 meta-analysis found a substantial one, and this disagreement is driven largely by real differences across echinacea species, plant parts, and preparations that make results from one commercial product hard to generalize to another.

claims.useCase: Preventing or shortening the common cold and upper respiratory infections (oral supplement; effect varies meaningfully by species and preparation)
claims.gradeRationale: Three independent reviews point the same general direction but disagree sharply on magnitude and significance. The 2014 Cochrane review (Karsch-Volk et al., 24 trials, 4,631 participants, 33 comparisons) found no statistically significant difference in any of 12 individual prevention comparisons, with only a post-hoc pooled estimate suggesting a 10-20% relative risk reduction, and only 2 of 6 treatment-duration comparisons reaching significance; Cochrane explicitly declined to pool its main analysis due to 'strong clinical heterogeneity' across echinacea species, plant parts, and preparation methods. A 2007 meta-analysis (Shah et al., 14 trials, verified via the NIH/AHRQ DARE database) found a much larger and statistically significant effect (pooled OR 0.42 for catching a cold, about a 58% odds reduction; 1.44 fewer days of illness), though its own reviewers note the duration effect lost significance when looking at echinacea-alone trials rather than combination products. A third review (David & Cunningham 2019, 29 RCTs reviewed/16 pooled, verified via McMaster's structured summary) found a more modest 12-22% reduction in catching a cold with no effect on duration, closer to Cochrane's cautious framing. NCCIH's own summary lands closest to Cochrane: echinacea 'may slightly reduce your chances of catching a cold,' with the effect on duration 'unclear.' Graded C: a consistent small positive direction for prevention across three independent reviews, but the most recent and methodologically conservative of the three found no significant effect in any individual comparison, and real species/preparation variability across commercial products means a given product's effect cannot be assumed from these pooled results.

Topical use for wounds and skin conditions has real traditional roots (NCCIH notes Native Americans used echinacea for respiratory infections, tooth pain, and snakebite) but modern supporting evidence is limited to animal and in-vitro wound-healing studies plus an uncontrolled historical case series, none of which constitutes controlled human clinical evidence. safetyNotes.text: Echinacea can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe, including rare cases of asthma and anaphylaxis; people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, daisies, or other plants in the Asteraceae family may be at higher risk of cross-reactivity. Anyone with these allergies should use caution.

People with autoimmune disorders (such as lupus or multiple sclerosis), advanced HIV infection, tuberculosis, or organ transplants should avoid echinacea, since it may stimulate T-cell activity. Echinacea may also make immunosuppressant medications like tacrolimus and cyclosporine less effective, and may reduce the effectiveness of some anticancer medications; anyone on these medications should talk with a healthcare provider before use.

Rare cases of liver injury, including self-limited hepatitis and cholestatic injury, have been reported with echinacea, though controlled trials have not linked it to liver injury and major hepatotoxicity reviews largely do not mention it, underscoring its rarity. Anyone who develops unexplained fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, or dark urine while taking echinacea should stop use and seek care.

Echinacea's effect on CYP3A4-metabolized drugs is complex and not consistently one direction, appearing to induce the liver enzyme while inhibiting the intestinal form at the same time; this can affect drugs including some chemotherapy agents and HIV antiretrovirals. Anyone taking a CYP3A4-metabolized medication should talk with a healthcare provider before combining it with echinacea.
Common mild side effects include gastrointestinal upset, headache, dizziness, and rash.

Some echinacea extracts are described as possibly safe for up to 7 days during the first trimester of pregnancy, but data are limited and a provider should be consulted first; little is known about safety while breastfeeding.
Echinacea is possibly safe for short-term use in children, but rashes (possibly allergic) have been reported in a clinical trial, so a provider should be consulted before use.

Echinacea products vary substantially by species (at least 9 recognized species), plant part used, and preparation method (fresh-pressed juice, alcohol tincture, dried extract), and this variability affects both how well a given product works and how directly research on one product applies to another; treat results from one commercial echinacea product with caution when generalizing to a different one.

name: Elderberry
summary: A dark purple berry from the elder shrub, traditionally cooked into syrups and jams and now most studied as a standardized supplement (syrup, lozenge, or extract) taken to ease the duration and severity of cold and flu symptoms; raw, unripe, or unprocessed parts of the plant are toxic and must never be eaten.

claims.useCase: Reducing the duration and severity of cold and flu symptoms once illness has started (standardized elderberry syrup or extract, e.g. Sambucol-style products)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH notes a small number of studies have evaluated elderberry for colds, flu, and other upper respiratory infections, with preliminary research suggesting it may relieve symptoms. A 2021 GRADE-assessed systematic review (Wieland et al.) found elderberry extract was associated with a shorter mean cold duration (about 2 days shorter) and lower symptom-severity scores than placebo in one small trial, and roughly 2.7 days faster overall symptom resolution/improvement in influenza across two small trials, compared with placebo. However, the review rated the certainty of every one of these individual effect estimates as very low, citing risk of bias and imprecision from small sample sizes, and rated the overall body of evidence across outcomes as moderate to very low certainty. All five trials included in that review were sponsored by the manufacturer of the specific product being tested (for example Iprona AG for the cold trial, and Razei Bar — maker of Sambucol — for the influenza trials), a funding pattern the review's own risk-of-bias assessment factored into its low-certainty ratings. Graded C: a fairly consistent direction of benefit for symptom duration and severity across several independent small trials, but limited confidence given trial size, quality concerns, and manufacturer funding of the underlying studies.

claims.useCase: Reducing the likelihood of developing a cold when taken proactively, e.g. before or during travel or known exposure
claims.gradeRationale: The only trial in the Wieland et al. (2021) systematic review that tested this specific use (a 312-person air-travel trial) found fewer elderberry-group participants developed a cold than placebo-group participants, but the difference was not statistically significant (12/154 vs. 17/158; risk ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.34-1.39, p = 0.30), and the review rated the certainty of this estimate as low due to risk of bias and imprecision. This is a different and currently weaker evidence question than the symptom-duration/severity claim above (which applies once illness has already begun): existing evidence does not clearly show elderberry lowers the odds of getting sick in the first place. Left ungraded given the single small trial and non-significant result.

citations.label: PMC: Elderberry for prevention and treatment of viral respiratory illnesses — a systematic review (Wieland et al., 2021)

claims.useCase: General immune-system support (non-specific supplement or tonic use, outside of active cold/flu symptoms)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states there isn't enough information to show whether elderberry is helpful for any health purpose beyond the limited cold/flu symptom research described above, and specifically notes elderberry has also been marketed for use against COVID-19 with no good evidence to support that use, leading the FDA and FTC to take action against companies making unsubstantiated effectiveness claims. Left ungraded: broad immune-support marketing language is not itself a specific, evidence-tested use case.

safetyNotes.text: Raw or unripe elderberries, and other parts of the elder plant such as the leaves, stems, bark, and roots, contain cyanide-producing (cyanogenic) compounds that can cause nausea, vomiting, and severe diarrhea; large amounts of the toxin may cause serious illness. Cooking destroys this toxin, so only properly cooked ripe berries or commercial extracts/syrups made from them should be used — raw or unripe elderberry, or any other part of the plant, should never be eaten.

Even with prepared elderberry supplements, consumer complaints reported to the FDA most commonly describe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; rare case reports of more serious reactions, including acute pancreatitis, have also been described in people taking elderberry products.

Elderberry has documented immune-stimulating effects, including increased production of some inflammatory cytokines in small human and lab studies, leading some secondary sources to advise caution for people with autoimmune conditions (such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus) or those taking medication that suppresses the immune system, since it could theoretically work against how those medications are intended to function. A single published case report describes a woman on long-term elderberry supplements who developed autoimmune hepatitis, though the authors describe the link as plausible rather than confirmed and did not re-expose her to elderberry to test causality. A 2021 systematic review found no clinical-trial evidence of elderberry causing harmful immune overstimulation or a cytokine-storm-type reaction, but noted the underlying research on this question is limited.

Secondary sources note elderberry may add to the effect of diuretics (raising dehydration risk), may lower blood sugar and add to the effect of diabetes medications (raising hypoglycemia risk), may reduce blood levels of the asthma drug theophylline, may add to the effect of other laxatives, and have flagged a possible interaction with chemotherapy drugs. Talk to a healthcare provider before combining elderberry with any of these.

There is essentially no human safety data on elderberry use during pregnancy; a dedicated literature review found no identified safety studies (human or animal) at all and recommended against using elderberry for upper-respiratory symptoms during pregnancy, given the combination of no safety data and only a small efficacy evidence base (77 total participants across three small trials). NIH's LactMed database similarly reports no data on whether elderberry components pass into breastmilk or on its safety for nursing infants, so no recommendation can currently be made for medicinal-dose elderberry use while breastfeeding.

name: Fenugreek
summary: An aromatic legume seed long used in South Asian and Middle Eastern cooking and traditional medicine, most studied today as an oral supplement for blood-sugar support in type 2 diabetes, where trial-level evidence is real but consistently rated low quality, and, with more mixed and often small or high-risk-of-bias evidence, for supporting breast-milk supply during lactation, modestly influencing cholesterol and lipid levels, and raising total testosterone in men. It carries meaningful allergy and cross-reactivity risk as a legume related to peanuts and chickpeas, and can compound the blood-sugar-lowering and bleeding-risk effects of diabetes medications and anticoagulants.

claims.useCase: Blood glucose / glycemic control in type 2 diabetes (oral fenugreek seed supplement)
claims.gradeRationale: Three independent sources (NCCIH, a 2014 meta-analysis of 10 trials/278 participants, and a 2026 systematic review) agree fenugreek lowers fasting glucose, postprandial glucose, and HbA1c, with the HbA1c pooled result showing no heterogeneity across 3 trials. But every source, including the review authors themselves, independently describes trial quality as generally poor (no reporting of randomization or allocation-concealment methods) and flags substantial heterogeneity on the fasting- and postload-glucose outcomes, plus a very wide effective-dose range (1-100 g/day) across trials.

claims.useCase: Lactation / breast-milk supply support (galactagogue)
claims.gradeRationale: The single most famous traditional use of this herb, yet the two most rigorous sources found - a 2026 systematic review restricted to controlled trials and the NIH's own LactMed monograph - both land on insufficient/mixed evidence, and the largest isolated-fenugreek RCT (n=26) found a negative, non-significant point estimate for milk volume at day 10, not just a null result. Left ungraded rather than assigned a low letter grade because the evidence base is too thin (two small, high-risk-of-bias RCTs) to grade confidently in either direction.

claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH's own page does not address this use case at all. A 2026 systematic review found fenugreek's lipid effect distinctly smaller and less consistent than its glycemic effect (3 of 8 lipid-assessing studies reached significance, versus a much stronger showing for guar gum). The most rigorous single RCT found significant within-group cholesterol and LDL-c reductions, but the same comparisons versus placebo did not reach significance, and the authors themselves characterized the effect size as small to trivial. Left ungraded given how inconsistent the between-group evidence is.

claims.gradeRationale: A 2026 meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (385 participants) found a small but statistically significant pooled effect on total testosterone with zero heterogeneity across trials, but free testosterone showed no significant effect and substantial heterogeneity. Across all 13 included trials, none was rated low risk of bias, and GRADE certainty for both primary outcomes was rated 'very low.' The review authors explicitly flagged common industry sponsorship and suspected publication bias, and concluded the evidence does not support commercial testosterone-boosting marketing claims.

claims.useCase: Appetite / satiety support
claims.gradeRationale: A single small (n=9), randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial found fenugreek tea significantly reduced subjective hunger and increased fullness ratings, but the most clinically meaningful outcome - actual food intake at a subsequent buffet - fell just short of statistical significance (p=0.06). No systematic review, meta-analysis, or independent replication was found. Left ungraded as a preliminary single-trial signal.

claims.useCase: Traditional topical scalp use and PCOS-related hair loss support
claims.gradeRationale: Topical scalp use of fenugreek paste is documented only as historical/traditional practice, with no controlled-trial evidence found. A single small comparative RCT found oral fenugreek non-inferior in safety to metformin for PCOS-related hair loss in women, but it was not placebo-controlled, reported no quantified effect size, and its individual risk-of-bias rating could not be isolated from the wider review. Left ungraded as a preliminary lead, not an established use.

safetyNotes.text: Fenugreek is a legume (Fabaceae family) and carries a real, sometimes severe allergy and cross-reactivity risk, especially for people with peanut, pea, or chickpea allergies. Case reports document reactions ranging from rhinitis and urticaria to anaphylaxis (facial flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, shortness of breath) and, in one case, Stevens-Johnson syndrome in a postpartum woman using fenugreek for lactation. Overall, fatalities are not reported and most reactions are described as mild and self-limiting, but anyone with a legume allergy should use caution.

Fenugreek has a real blood-sugar-lowering effect and can compound the effect of diabetes medications, with a documented case of hypoglycemia in a patient on metformin after 12 weeks of fenugreek capsules. NCCIH separately warns large doses may cause a harmful drop in blood sugar. Anyone on insulin or an oral hypoglycemic medication should consult a healthcare provider and monitor blood sugar closely before using fenugreek.

Multiple independent sources (LiverTox, a scoping review documenting a rising INR in a patient on warfarin, MSKCC, and LactMed) flag a bleeding-risk interaction with anticoagulant and antiplatelet medications, particularly warfarin. One case involved a co-administered second herb (Boldo) rather than fenugreek alone, and a case of severe clotting failure was reported in a patient with cirrhosis using excessive amounts of fenugreek milk porridge. Anyone on warfarin or another anticoagulant/antiplatelet medication should talk with a healthcare provider before using fenugreek.

NCCIH states fenugreek is not safe to use during pregnancy in amounts greater than those found in food, and that use has been linked to increased risk of birth defects in both animal and human data; MSKCC corroborates this independently. Neither source specifies an exact mechanism.

Culinary, food-level amounts of fenugreek are FDA-recognized as safe (GRAS) and several controlled studies found no difference in infant adverse events between fenugreek and control groups, but data on larger galactagogue-level doses remain limited; an Australian survey found 17% of breastfeeding mothers taking fenugreek reported adverse reactions such as stomach cramps, nausea, and body odor. Fenugreek's compound sotolon commonly and harmlessly gives urine, sweat, and possibly breastmilk a 'maple syrup' odor in both mother and infant - this is benign but has been mistaken for maple syrup urine disease, a serious genetic disorder, prompting unnecessary medical workup in newborns.

Two independent case reports describe serotonin syndrome symptoms (hyperreflexia, nausea, anxiety, tachycardia) in breastfeeding women on the SSRI sertraline who used fenugreek to support milk supply. This is a specific, documented interaction relevant to postpartum patients on SSRIs.

A scoping review found fenugreek consumption associated with reduced serum potassium, with increased risk when combined with diuretics or other potassium-lowering drugs. This is currently single-sourced; NCCIH and MSKCC did not mention this caution in the content reviewed.

Gastrointestinal upset (diarrhea, nausea, reflux, bloating, abdominal pain) is the most frequently reported adverse effect of fenugreek, corroborated independently by NCCIH and a scoping review of case reports, including several diarrhea/bloating cases in a type 1 diabetes trial.

MSKCC notes theoretical/animal-data-only interaction concerns with cyclophosphamide (a chemotherapy drug) and altered theophylline bioavailability in an animal model, and a scoping review cautions fenugreek's fiber content may interfere with absorption of concurrently administered oral medications, particularly those with a narrow therapeutic index. These are lower-confidence, largely preclinical cautions rather than confirmed human interactions.

The NIH's LiverTox monograph assigns fenugreek Likelihood Category E (unlikely cause of clinically apparent liver injury); a DILIN study of US liver-injury cases linked to herbal supplements found none attributed to fenugreek, and animal research suggests possible hepatoprotective activity. A separately reported case of severe clotting failure in a cirrhosis patient using excessive fenugreek milk porridge reflects a bleeding-related complication in a patient with pre-existing liver disease, not evidence of fenugreek-caused liver injury.

As a dietary supplement, fenugreek is not tested or approved by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale, and product content may vary from labeling, so results from one product or preparation may not generalize to others.

Laboratory research cited by MSKCC found fenugreek acted as an estrogen receptor modulator and stimulated breast cancer cells in vitro; patients with hormone-sensitive cancers are advised to consult their physicians before using fenugreek. This is a single-sourced, laboratory-level finding, not a documented human clinical outcome.

name: Feverfew
summary: A daisy-family plant whose dried leaves have long been used in folk medicine for fevers, headache, and menstrual complaints, but which is studied today almost entirely as an oral supplement for migraine prevention. The best available evidence, a Cochrane systematic review of 6 placebo-controlled trials, describes this as a genuine but low-quality and inconsistent signal: real in the largest, most rigorous trial, absent in several others. A formal rheumatoid-arthritis trial found essentially no benefit. Feverfew carries several real safety considerations, including a documented 'post-feverfew syndrome' of rebound symptoms after abruptly stopping long-term use, ragweed/Asteraceae cross-allergy risk, mouth ulcers from chewing raw leaves, and a bleeding-risk/anticoagulant caution supported by a detailed case report.

claims.useCase: Migraine prevention (oral leaf extract/powder)
claims.gradeRationale: A Cochrane systematic review of 6 double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs (561 total participants) found genuinely mixed individual trial results: two trials showed a significant benefit, one of them (Diener 2005, the largest and most rigorous, n=170) finding migraine frequency fell by a net 0.6 attacks/month versus placebo (p=0.0456); other trials, including the second-largest (Pfaffenrath 2002, n=147) and de Weerdt 1996 (n=44), found no significant effect. Sample-size-related bias was rated unclear or high risk in all six included trials. The review authors' own verbatim conclusion: 'low quality evidence that feverfew is effective in migraine prevention.' NCCIH corroborates the same 'inconsistent findings, but some research indicates a reduction in frequency' framing, and MSKCC independently describes the overall evidence as 'mixed.'

claims.useCase: Rheumatoid arthritis / joint pain
claims.gradeRationale: Evidence here is essentially negative, not merely weak. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 41 women with rheumatoid arthritis, reported in a systematic review, found only 1 of 15 measured clinical parameters (grip strength) improved significantly versus placebo. RxList independently rates feverfew for rheumatoid arthritis symptoms 'Possibly Ineffective,' a stronger, more specific negative rating than its general 'Insufficient Evidence' catch-all used for most other traditional uses. Left ungraded and presented as traditional use with essentially negative modern trial evidence, in contrast to the migraine claim above.

safetyNotes.text: 'Post-feverfew syndrome': stopping long-term regular use abruptly can trigger rebound migraine along with joint/muscle aches, anxiety, headache, nausea, and vomiting. This is documented directly in a primary Cochrane-reviewed trial and corroborated independently by two reference sources listing overlapping symptoms (headaches, insomnia, joint pain, nervousness, poor sleep patterns, stiffness, tension, tiredness). Recommend tapering rather than abruptly stopping after regular, longer-term use.
Cross-allergy risk for people allergic to ragweed or other Asteraceae/Compositae-family plants (chrysanthemums, marigolds, and similar). Corroborated independently across NCCIH, MSKCC, and RxList.

Bleeding risk / anticoagulant and antiplatelet interaction (aspirin, warfarin, ibuprofen, naproxen, heparin, and similar). Feverfew's active constituent parthenolide inhibits platelet activity through multiple pathways. Both MSKCC and RxList rate the clinical interaction as 'Moderate,' with clinical relevance described by MSKCC as 'unknown' — the elevated severity here reflects a directly on-point published case report (Naranjo score 8, 'probable') of a patient on feverfew 800 mg 2-3x/day for 6+ months who developed prolonged PT/PTT and abnormal vaginal bleeding that resolved after stopping feverfew, rather than the reference sources' own moderate rating. NCCIH and RxList both recommend discontinuing feverfew at least 2 weeks before scheduled surgery.

Possible CYP450 drug-metabolism interactions (CYP1A2, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4), which could affect drugs including warfarin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, and propranolol. MSKCC and RxList both describe this qualitatively as a 'Moderate' theoretical risk, but both explicitly caveat that human clinical significance is not firmly established.

Not recommended during pregnancy: feverfew may affect uterine contractions, with RxList rating pregnancy use 'Possibly Unsafe' due to risk of early contractions and miscarriage. Also not recommended while breastfeeding or for children, due to insufficient safety data. Corroborated independently across NCCIH, RxList, and a systematic review.

Chewing raw/fresh leaves can cause mouth ulcers, mouth sores, and swelling — distinct from, and riskier than, standard short-term oral-supplement use (which is generally well tolerated). A systematic review's user survey found 18% of users reported adverse effects, with mouth ulceration in 11% being the single most common effect.
Topical use can cause contact dermatitis, including a documented case of exacerbated dermatitis following use of a moisturizer containing feverfew.

Mild gastrointestinal side effects with standard oral use (nausea, digestive upset, bloating, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, flatulence). Trial-level Cochrane data found adverse events across 6 RCTs were generally mild and reversible, with three of six trials actually finding higher adverse-event rates in the placebo arm than the feverfew arm, and no serious treatment-related adverse events in any trial.

No dedicated LiverTox monograph exists for feverfew (confirmed via direct index check, not just a failed URL guess), so no LiverTox-sourced liver-safety assessment, positive or negative, can be made. None of the other sources reviewed (NCCIH, MSKCC, RxList, systematic reviews) reported a hepatotoxicity signal either.

One study of chronic feverfew users over 11 months found no induced chromosomal abnormalities, but the same review notes no chronic toxicity studies exist, so long-term safety beyond that single study remains unestablished. Single-sourced and explicitly caveated by its own source as an incomplete evidence base.

As a dietary supplement, feverfew is not pre-approved by the FDA for safety or efficacy before sale, and commercial products may vary in parthenolide content — the Cochrane review itself calls for future trials to use stable, standardized extracts given inconsistency across the products used in the trials it reviewed.

name: Garlic
summary: A widely used culinary bulb also sold as a concentrated supplement for cardiovascular health; multiple meta-analyses find modest, consistent reductions in cholesterol and blood pressure (the latter specifically in people who already have hypertension), though the most methodologically rigorous historical analysis found the cholesterol effect became nonsignificant among only the highest-quality trials, and no study has shown garlic supplements actually reduce heart attacks or strokes.

claims.useCase: Lowering total cholesterol and LDL in people with elevated cholesterol (oral supplement, more than 2 months of use)
claims.gradeRationale: Multiple independent meta-analyses converge on a modest, statistically significant reduction. Ried, Toben & Fakler 2013 (39 trials pooled) found total cholesterol reduced by 17 +/- 6 mg/dL and LDL by 9 +/- 6 mg/dL with more than 2 months of use in people with elevated cholesterol, with HDL improved only slightly and triglycerides not significantly affected. Two more recent meta-analyses corroborate a similar direction and magnitude: a 2024 analysis (PMID 38892625) found total cholesterol down 14.17 mg/dL and LDL down 8.20 mg/dL; a 2025/2026 analysis pooling 108 trials (PMID 40580481) found total cholesterol down 10.21 mg/dL and LDL down 5.90 mg/dL. However, an earlier, more methodologically rigorous analysis (Stevinson, Pittler & Ernst 2000, 13 RCTs) found that after removing one outlier trial, or restricting to the 5 trials using an identical standardized preparation, or restricting to only the 6 highest-quality trials, the effect became nonsignificant in every case — leading those authors to conclude garlic's cholesterol effect is 'of questionable value' and 'may not be clinically meaningful.' No trial has measured actual cardiovascular events; a risk-equation extrapolation from Ried 2013 estimating a '38% reduction in coronary events' is a modeled projection from the cholesterol change, not an observed trial outcome. Graded C: a consistent modest positive direction across several independent meta-analyses, but the most quality-conscious historical analysis found no significant effect among its best-evidence trial subsets, and no trial has confirmed a downstream reduction in actual cardiovascular events.

claims.useCase: Lowering blood pressure specifically in people with hypertension (oral supplement)
claims.gradeRationale: Two meta-analyses from an overlapping author group (Ried, Frank & Stocks 2008, 11 studies; Ried, Travica & Sali 2016, 20 trials/970 participants) both found no meaningful blood-pressure effect in normotensive people, but a real, consistent reduction specifically in people who already have hypertension: the 2008 analysis found systolic blood pressure down 8.4 +/- 2.8 mmHg and diastolic down 7.3 +/- 1.5 mmHg in the hypertensive subgroup (both p<0.001); the 2016 update found systolic down 8.7 +/- 2.2 mmHg and diastolic down 6.1 +/- 1.3 mmHg in the hypertensive subgroup (both p<0.001). Two more recent, independent 2025 meta-analyses point the same direction with smaller effect sizes: a dose-response aged-garlic-extract analysis (PMID 40628369) found systolic down 2.49 mmHg, and a hypertensive-only analysis (PMID 41393949) found systolic down 4.21 mmHg and diastolic down 3.13 mmHg. NCCIH's own framing is consistent but more cautious: 'limited evidence suggests that garlic supplements may reduce blood pressure to a small extent in people who have high blood pressure.' Graded C: a real and fairly consistent effect confined to people with hypertension, replicated across two research groups, but much of the underlying meta-analytic work comes from one overlapping author group (Ried et al.), the primary trials feeding it are generally small and short, and no trial has confirmed that this blood-pressure effect translates into fewer actual cardiovascular events.

claims.useCase: Slowing coronary calcium (atherosclerosis) progression (aged garlic extract, small imaging-surrogate trials)
claims.gradeRationale: Two small pilot trials of a proprietary aged-garlic-extract product found slower progression of coronary artery calcium score, an imaging surrogate for atherosclerosis, versus placebo. Budoff et al. 2004 (n=19 completers, all also on statin therapy, 1 year) found calcium score increased 7.5% with aged garlic extract versus 22.2% with placebo (p=0.046). A 2013 trial from the same research group (n=60, 12 months) found significantly lower calcium-score progression, but used a compound product combining aged garlic extract with B12, folic acid, B6, and L-arginine, so the effect cannot be cleanly attributed to garlic alone. Both trials are small, used a specific proprietary aged-garlic-extract preparation rather than raw garlic or garlic powder, and measured a surrogate imaging marker rather than an actual cardiovascular event; no larger outcome trial has been conducted. Left ungraded: this is preliminary, mechanistically supportive evidence, too thin and too confounded for a letter grade.

claims.useCase: Preventing the common cold (oral supplement)
claims.gradeRationale: A Cochrane systematic review (Lissiman, Bhasale & Cohen, most recent update 2014) found only one trial ever met its inclusion criteria across three successive review updates spanning 2009 to 2014: a 146-participant trial of a daily allicin-containing garlic capsule over 12 weeks found fewer cold occurrences with garlic (24) than placebo (65, p<0.001) and fewer total sick days, though once a cold did occur its duration was similar between groups. Cochrane's own conclusion is direct: 'there is insufficient clinical trial evidence regarding the effects of garlic in preventing or treating the common cold... more studies are needed,' adding that effectiveness claims 'appear to rely largely on poor-quality evidence.' NCCIH separately notes a 2022 systematic review 'identified only two studies that suggest a possible benefit, and both studies included only small numbers of people and had weaknesses in the research.' Left ungraded: a single small trial repeatedly re-cited over more than a decade with no second qualifying trial, and Cochrane's own explicit conclusion of insufficient evidence.

claims.useCase: Reducing cancer risk (stomach, colorectal)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states garlic consumption 'does not seem to reduce risk of stomach cancer,' and that it's 'uncertain whether garlic influences risk of colorectal cancer.' A meta-analysis of 11 observational studies (Zhou, Qian, Zhang & Zeng 2020, 12,558 cases) found an overall protective association for colorectal cancer (RR 0.80), but this split inconsistently by study design: case-control studies showed a protective association (RR 0.71) while cohort studies, generally the stronger observational design, showed an essentially null result (RR 0.99, confidence interval crossing 1). This is observational association data, not causal trial evidence, and even that association is inconsistent depending on study design. Left ungraded: observational only, inconsistent by design, and NCCIH itself is unconvinced for stomach cancer and calls colorectal cancer risk uncertain.

safetyNotes.text: Garlic supplements may increase the risk of bleeding, an effect that appears independent of whether someone is also taking a blood thinner. A supplement-surgery bleeding review found garlic strongly associated with surgical bleeding, among the strongest of over 20 supplements reviewed, and recommends stopping nonessential supplements 2 weeks before surgery; a separate source recommends discontinuing garlic at least 1-2 weeks before surgery. Anyone about to have surgery, or taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication (including aspirin), should talk with a healthcare provider about stopping garlic supplements beforehand.

Garlic's interaction with warfarin specifically is not as clear-cut as its general bleeding-risk profile might suggest. One controlled human study of an enteric-coated garlic tablet found no significant effect on platelet aggregation or on warfarin's levels in the body, and older case reports of bleeding linked to garlic did not clearly involve patients taking warfarin. Even so, a consumer drug-interaction database rates garlic plus warfarin a Moderate interaction, noting garlic might increase warfarin's effectiveness and the combination might increase the chances of bruising and bleeding. Given the mixed direct evidence but real theoretical mechanism (garlic's antiplatelet activity), anyone on warfarin should use caution and have their levels monitored if combining it with garlic supplements.

Garlic supplements substantially reduce blood levels of the HIV protease inhibitor saquinavir. A controlled pharmacokinetic study found garlic reduced saquinavir's overall drug exposure by 51%, trough levels by 49%, and peak levels by 54%, with levels recovering to only 60-70% of baseline even 10 days after stopping garlic. A secondary source also reports garlic significantly reducing darunavir levels, with case reports of viral rebound attributed to sub-therapeutic darunavir levels while on garlic, though this specific darunavir claim was not independently verified against a primary case report. Anyone taking HIV protease inhibitor medications should avoid garlic supplements or use only under close medical supervision.

Garlic may reduce absorption of the antibiotic isoniazid; a consumer drug-interaction database rates this a Major interaction and advises against combining them. Garlic may also add to the effect of other blood-thinning medications (aspirin, clopidogrel, ibuprofen, heparin), drugs metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP2E1 (including some calcium-channel blockers, anesthesia, antifungal, and cancer drugs), and other blood-pressure-lowering medications, given garlic's own blood-pressure-lowering effect. A single source additionally reports garlic reducing cyclosporine's effectiveness with a risk of transplant rejection, and garlic may lower blood sugar enough to require an insulin dose adjustment. Anyone on these medications should talk with a healthcare provider before combining them with garlic supplements.
Common side effects of fresh raw garlic include body odor, abdominal pain, gas, and nausea; some people have allergic reactions to garlic.
Applying raw garlic directly to the skin can cause burns and irritation; it should not be applied undiluted to skin.

Garlic may not be safe to use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding when taken orally in amounts greater than those typically found in food, i.e., concentrated supplement doses rather than culinary use.

name: Ginger
summary: A pungent flowering-plant rhizome long used in Asian cooking and traditional medicine, most studied today as an oral supplement for nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy, where evidence is comparatively strong; evidence is more mixed and lower-quality for chemotherapy-related and post-surgery nausea and for knee osteoarthritis pain, where ginger consistently underperforms comparator herbs like Boswellia and turmeric in head-to-head data. It carries a real, if not fully quantified, bleeding-risk caution relevant to anyone on blood thinners or facing surgery.

claims.useCase: Nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy (morning sickness), oral supplement
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states plainly that 'research shows that ginger may be helpful for nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy.' A systematic review and meta-analysis (Viljoen et al. 2014, 12 RCTs, 1,278 pregnant women) found ginger significantly reduced nausea versus placebo/comparators (MD 1.20, 95% CI 0.56-1.84, p=0.0002) with low heterogeneity across trials, but did not significantly reduce vomiting specifically (MD 0.72, 95% CI -0.03-1.46, p=0.06) with substantial heterogeneity between trials. The same review found a miscarriage-risk point estimate that was not statistically significant but came with a wide confidence interval (RR 3.14, 95% CI 0.65-15.11) that cannot fully rule out increased risk; the authors themselves caveat their overall conclusion, calling the evidence 'limited' and 'low quality' despite describing ginger as 'a harmless and possibly effective alternative option.' Trial doses across the pooled studies ranged 600-2,500 mg/day, mostly clustering around 1,000 mg/day, with doses under 1,500 mg/day trending more effective than higher doses. ACOG's Practice Bulletin No. 189 on nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (per a guideline-aggregator summary of the bulletin) grades ginger as a nonpharmacologic option at ACOG evidence Level B. A more conservative source, MSKCC, states ginger supplements 'should be avoided during pregnancy or lactation' since effects on gestational development are unknown, and notes the German Commission E contraindicates ginger for morning sickness during pregnancy — a real, worth-naming conflict with NCCIH and ACOG's more permissive framing, likely reflecting MSKCC's more conservative oncology-context orientation. Graded B: a genuine, statistically significant, low-heterogeneity nausea benefit across over a thousand pregnant women, corroborated by NCCIH and an ACOG practice-bulletin recommendation, is the strongest and best-corroborated use case researched for this herb — but not graded higher given the non-significant vomiting outcome, the too-wide-to-be-reassuring miscarriage-risk confidence interval, the reviewers' own 'low quality' rating, and a real conflicting conservative source. Anyone pregnant should talk with a healthcare provider before using ginger supplements rather than self-dosing.

claims.useCase: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, as an adjunct to standard antiemetics
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH's own framing is uncertain: 'it's uncertain whether ginger is a helpful addition to standard treatments for nausea and vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy.' Two systematic reviews published the same year disagree. Choi et al. 2022 (23 RCTs across cancer types) found no significant pooled effect on acute nausea, delayed nausea, or delayed vomiting, and only a borderline effect on overall acute vomiting (p=0.09); one dose/duration subgroup (at most 1 g/day for more than 4 days) did show a significant roughly 70% reduction in acute-vomiting odds, but individual trial results were explicitly inconsistent, and the authors rated overall evidence certainty 'very low.' A narrower review restricted to breast cancer patients (2022, pooling 4 of 5 identified RCTs, 337 patients) found a significant reduction in overall, acute, and delayed CINV severity, with no serious adverse events. Both reviews flag high heterogeneity and call for more rigorous trials. Left ungraded given this genuine disagreement between two similarly-sized systematic reviews published the same year and NCCIH's own 'uncertain' framing.

claims.useCase: Post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV), oral supplement
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH describes ginger's effect on nausea and vomiting after surgery as uncertain, in the same breath as its chemotherapy-nausea uncertainty. Two independent, more recent reviews corroborate a consistently weak-to-null signal specifically on incidence. Anh et al. 2020 (109-RCT comprehensive review, 11 RCTs specifically on PONV) found 5 of those RCTs showed no significant result, with some benefit suggested only in gynecological-surgery subpopulations, and concluded results were 'inconsistent between studies even with a comparatively high dose.' Ha et al. 2024 (a laparoscopic-surgery review, 9 ginger-only RCTs within it) found no significant difference between ginger and placebo on nausea incidence at 24 hours (RR 0.79, p=0.19) or vomiting incidence at 24 hours (RR 0.81, p=0.50); a positive finding on nausea severity at 12 hours (SMD -2.04, p=0.01) came with very high heterogeneity (I-squared=97%) that limits confidence in it. Ginger also showed no significant difference against standard antiemetic drugs on either nausea or vomiting incidence. Left ungraded: across NCCIH and two independent recent systematic reviews, incidence-outcome data consistently lands on 'not significant,' a more consistently weak picture than the pregnancy-nausea use case.
