claims.useCase: Knee osteoarthritis and joint pain (oral supplement)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states ginger supplements 'might be helpful for symptoms of knee osteoarthritis, but much of the research has been of poor quality,' and that topical ginger 'has not been shown to be helpful' for the same use. Anh et al. 2020's comprehensive review found 6 osteoarthritis studies, all reporting improvement on some measure versus control, but results against NSAIDs directly conflicted between trials (one found ginger as effective as ibuprofen, another found the opposite). A 2025 placebo-controlled trial (Broeckel et al., 30 completers) found significant reductions on some inflammatory markers and pain/stiffness improvements at some follow-up points, but its primary overall outcome measure (WOMAC) was not significant (p=0.690), and mild side effects (headache, heart palpitations, nervousness) were reported more often with ginger than placebo. A 2025 network meta-analysis comparing 7 nutritional supplements for knee osteoarthritis (Zhang et al.) found ginger reached significance only on the VAS pain outcome, not on WOMAC pain, stiffness, or function, and ranked ginger mid-pack, consistently outperformed by Boswellia (which topped every outcome) and generally outperformed by curcumin/turmeric as well; the review also flagged a high likelihood of publication bias. Left ungraded: real trial-level evidence exists, more than for post-surgical nausea, but it is consistently smaller in magnitude and less consistently significant than for comparator botanicals tested in the same reviews.

safetyNotes.text: Ginger may increase bleeding risk, an evolving and genuinely mixed area of evidence. An older (2000) systematic review found evidence lacking for a specific warfarin-ginger interaction, but a more recent (2021) systematic review lists ginger among herbs associated with reported bleeding events in warfarin patients, ranging from minor bruising to major bleeding; a consumer drug-interaction reference rates ginger plus warfarin a Moderate interaction and recommends regular blood monitoring. High-dose concentrated ginger (powder or tinctures) is separately noted to increase bleeding risk by decreasing platelet aggregation. Anyone on warfarin or another anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication should talk with a healthcare provider before using ginger supplements, especially at higher-than-culinary doses. Ginger should also be avoided by people with bleeding disorders and is often recommended to be stopped roughly 2 weeks before surgery as a precaution, though the underlying evidence for this specific timeframe is itself inconclusive.

Common side effects include abdominal discomfort, heartburn, diarrhea, and mouth and throat irritation. A large review of over 100 clinical trials found heartburn the only consistently reported symptom, occurring at doses of 500-2,000 mg/day, with no life-threatening or severe cases reported.
Ginger may increase the flow of bile and should be avoided by people with gallstones, per a single source (MSKCC); no second independent source corroborating this specific caution was found.

Ginger may cause larger reductions in blood sugar, risking an additive effect with diabetes medications; trial evidence shows ginger can significantly lower fasting blood sugar and HbA1c and improve insulin sensitivity in people with type 2 diabetes. Anyone on diabetes medication should monitor blood sugar closely and talk with a healthcare provider about possible dose adjustment.

Ginger may reduce blood pressure, risking an additive effect with blood pressure medications, particularly calcium-channel blockers; a consumer drug-interaction reference specifically flags the combination with nifedipine as a interaction to avoid. This caution is currently sourced to a single reference and was not independently corroborated by NCCIH or MSKCC.

No authoritative numeric dose ceiling exists for use during pregnancy. Commonly studied doses cluster around 1,000 mg/day; higher doses (1,500 mg/day or more) have not shown clearer benefit in trials and carry more bleeding and GI-upset concern. As with any supplement, discuss dosing with a healthcare provider before use during pregnancy.

Ginger has not been linked to serum enzyme elevations or clinically apparent liver injury in more than 100 clinical trials, and carries LiverTox's most reassuring Likelihood Category (E, 'unlikely cause of clinically apparent liver injury'); one isolated case report of acute liver injury with jaundice after a ginger-labeled product has been documented.
As with other dietary supplements, ginger products are not pre-approved by the FDA for safety or efficacy before sale.

summary: A minimally-processed tea leaf used for thousands of years, studied today for modest cholesterol and weight effects, and also the source material for sinecatechins (Veregen), an FDA-approved prescription ointment for genital and perianal warts.

safetyNotes.text: Concentrated tablet or capsule extracts have rarely been linked to liver injury; the brewed beverage has no such reports. People with a certain genetic variant, present in an estimated 5-15% of Americans, may be more susceptible.
Contains caffeine; extract supplements can cause nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort, or increased blood pressure.
May reduce blood levels of some medications, including the beta-blocker nadolol, the cholesterol medication atorvastatin, and the osteoporosis medication raloxifene.

NCCIH advises pregnant people to keep caffeine intake to moderate levels, and notes caffeine passes to a nursing infant through breast milk and can cause fussiness or poor sleep in the infant. MSKCC states this more categorically, advising against drinking green tea at all during pregnancy or while breastfeeding - both framings are reported here rather than picking one.

May reduce absorption of non-heme iron from food when green tea is consumed with meals; evidence is mixed, with an older controlled study finding reduced absorption and at least one later commentary disputing the effect. Worth a caution for anyone with or at risk of iron deficiency, rather than a well-established interaction.

MSKCC states that consuming large amounts of green tea may provide enough vitamin K to counteract the effects of anticoagulant medications such as warfarin; this was not independently found in NCCIH's own content, so treat it as a single-sourced but worth-mentioning caution for anyone on blood thinners.

name: Hawthorn
summary: A thorny shrub in the rose family whose leaves, flowers, and berries have a long history of traditional European use for the heart, most studied today as a standardized leaf-and-flower extract taken alongside conventional treatment for mild-to-moderate heart failure symptoms and exercise tolerance; it has not been shown in the largest, most rigorous trials to reduce heart failure mortality or major cardiac events, and it must never replace prescribed heart failure or cardiac medication.

claims.useCase: Exercise tolerance and heart failure symptoms such as breathlessness and fatigue (NYHA class I-III), as an add-on to conventional heart failure treatment (standardized leaf-and-flower extract, e.g. WS 1442 or LI 132)
claims.gradeRationale: A meta-analysis of 13 randomized, placebo-controlled trials (997 patients total) found hawthorn extract significantly increased maximal exercise workload versus placebo in a 4-trial, 310-patient subset (weighted mean difference 7 Watts, 95% CI 3-11, P<0.01); a broader pool of 8 trials/632 patients contributed to the meta-analysis's other pooled outcomes, including a significant improvement on the Zerssen symptom score (2 RCTs, 169 patients, WMD 6, 95% CI -9 to -2) and qualitative dyspnea/fatigue improvement reported separately across 4 RCTs. A 2010 clinical review in American Family Physician describes a subsequent 2008 Cochrane systematic review as reaching a similar conclusion on exercise tolerance and symptoms, and assigns hawthorn a SORT 'A' evidence rating for adjunct use in chronic heart failure based on these systematic reviews. However, that same review is explicit that there is 'no evidence of a notable reduction in mortality or sudden death,' and the underlying trials were short (mostly 3-16 weeks, typically 6-8 weeks). Two later, larger, and more rigorous trials complicate the picture further: the NCCIH-funded HERB-CHF trial (Zick et al., 2009; 120 patients, 6 months) found no significant benefit of hawthorn (WS 1442) over placebo on six-minute walk distance (P=0.61), quality of life, or functional capacity, with significantly more adverse events (mostly non-cardiac) reported in the hawthorn group (60% vs. 38%); and the large SPICE trial (2,681 patients, mean 24-month follow-up) found no significant difference between WS 1442 and placebo on its primary composite endpoint of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or hospitalization for worsening heart failure. Left ungraded: the pooled body of smaller, shorter, industry-associated trials shows a fairly consistent positive signal on symptoms and exercise tolerance, but this is genuinely contradicted by the largest and most methodologically rigorous individual trials available, so confidence in a real, durable symptom benefit is not high enough to assign a grade. Hawthorn is studied only as an addition to standard heart failure treatment, never as a replacement for it.

claims.useCase: Reducing heart failure mortality, hospitalization, or major cardiovascular events (e.g. cardiac death, myocardial infarction)
claims.gradeRationale: The largest and most rigorous trial to test this specific question, SPICE (2,681 adults with NYHA class II-III heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, randomized to Crataegus extract WS 1442 450 mg twice daily or placebo alongside standard heart failure therapy for a mean of 24 months across roughly 120 European centers), found no significant difference between hawthorn and placebo on its primary composite endpoint of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or hospitalization for progressive heart failure (27.9% vs. 28.9%, hazard ratio 0.95, not statistically significant), and no significant difference in cardiac death by study end (13.5% vs. 14.9%, p=0.269); an early reduction in cardiac death at 6 months (2.9% vs. 4.9%, p=0.009) did not persist through the full follow-up period. A separate published review of hawthorn's cardiovascular pharmacology independently corroborates that SPICE's primary endpoints 'were not achieved.' Total and serious adverse event rates were similar between the hawthorn and placebo groups (67.0% vs. 68.3% and 39.2% vs. 41.1%, respectively). Graded F: this is not merely an absence of evidence but a large, well-designed, placebo-controlled trial that specifically tested for, and did not find, a benefit on hard cardiac outcomes. Hawthorn should never be used as a strategy to try to reduce heart failure mortality, hospitalization, or major cardiac events in place of prescribed treatment.

claims.useCase: General traditional 'cardiotonic' use, and traditional/supplement use for mild anxiety or nervous tension
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH's overview states hawthorn is currently marketed for the heart and blood vessels, weight loss, and conditions such as anxiety, but that there is little or no quality evidence on hawthorn for most health conditions, with heart failure being essentially the only use that has been meaningfully studied in controlled human trials (addressed separately above). No controlled human trial evidence was found in this research for anxiety or general cardiotonic/tonic use specifically. Left ungraded: this reflects a long traditional-use history rather than any tested clinical use case.

safetyNotes.text: Hawthorn has inotropic (heart-muscle-stimulating) and vasodilatory effects that overlap mechanistically with some heart failure medications, including cardiac glycosides like digoxin. A small controlled study (Tankanow et al. 2003; 8 healthy volunteers, digoxin 0.25 mg/day alone versus combined with hawthorn WS 1442 450 mg twice daily for 3 weeks) found no statistically significant change in digoxin's pharmacokinetic parameters, and a pharmacology review describes this as supporting that the two 'may be co-administered safely.' However, that study was small, short, and conducted in healthy volunteers rather than people with heart failure, and RxList's consumer drug-interaction reference still rates combining hawthorn with digoxin a 'Moderate' interaction, advising against it without a doctor's direct supervision, given the overlapping mechanism and theoretical potential to add to digoxin's cardiac effects. Anyone taking digoxin or another cardiac glycoside should talk to their prescribing doctor before adding hawthorn rather than deciding on their own.

Hawthorn's vasodilatory and blood-pressure-lowering properties may add to the effects of antihypertensive and other heart failure or blood-pressure medications (including beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, and nitrates), raising the risk of excessively low blood pressure, dizziness, or lightheadedness. A clinical review describes interactions with antiarrhythmics, antihypertensives, digoxin, and antihyperlipidemic agents as theoretical and not yet substantiated by reported adverse events, but RxList separately rates combining hawthorn with nitrates a 'Major' interaction to avoid and rates beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers 'Moderate.' The same clinical review also flags caution when combining hawthorn with other herbs that have cardiac or blood-thinning activity, such as danshen, epimedium, ginger, ginseng, turmeric, and valerian, though specific interaction data for those combinations is limited. Anyone on blood-pressure or other heart medication should talk to a healthcare provider before adding hawthorn.

Hawthorn is studied only as a supplement alongside conventional heart failure treatment, never as a substitute for it. NCCIH states evidence on hawthorn's effects in people with heart failure is conflicting overall, and specifically flags one study in which a hawthorn preparation (C. oxycantha) appeared associated with earlier worsening of heart failure in participants, possibly related to an interaction with other medications they were taking. RxList separately notes that some specific branded hawthorn products (at doses of 160-1800 mg/day) have been linked to an increased risk of death or hospitalization for heart failure in at least one trial. Chest pain, breathlessness, swelling, or other possible symptoms of heart failure or heart disease should always be evaluated by a doctor promptly rather than self-managed with hawthorn.

In clinical trials, hawthorn is generally well tolerated. The most commonly reported side effects are dizziness/vertigo, nausea, and other gastrointestinal upset; less common reports include fatigue, sweating, palpitations, headache, breathlessness, sleep disturbance, agitation, and nosebleeds. The HERB-CHF trial reported significantly more adverse events overall in the hawthorn group than the placebo group, though most were described as non-cardiac.

There is little to no reliable human safety data on hawthorn use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. A clinical review advises against use during pregnancy due to a theoretical risk of stimulating uterine contractions, and against use while breastfeeding or in children given the lack of safety data; NCCIH similarly states that little is known about whether it's safe to use hawthorn during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

NCCIH notes that no research studies have tested whether it's safe to use hawthorn for longer than 16 weeks, so long-term safety is not established. As with other unstandardized botanical supplements, the concentration of active flavonoid and procyanidin compounds can vary between hawthorn products and manufacturers.

name: Licorice Root
summary: A legume-family root native to Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, used for millennia in Assyrian, Egyptian, Greek, Arab, Chinese, Tibetan, and Indian traditional medicine, most often for digestive discomfort, coughs and sore throat, and skin healing. Modern evidence is thin and mixed for most of these uses, but several small trials support topical licorice-derived preparations for eczema symptoms and licorice as an adjunct alongside standard therapy for H. pylori-related peptic ulcer. Its real safety concern is the active compound glycyrrhizin, which in high doses or with prolonged use can raise blood pressure and lower potassium seriously enough to affect heart rhythm, and which carries a documented risk to pregnancy outcomes when consumed heavily.

claims.useCase: Dyspepsia and general digestive discomfort (oral licorice)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states directly that it's unclear whether products containing licorice alone have an effect on digestive symptoms. MSKCC separately lists a traditional use for bloating, discomfort, nausea, and burping, and mentions a clinical-study benefit for dyspepsia, but without traceable trial detail. Left ungraded: the herb's own primary NCCIH source does not support a confident digestive-symptom claim, and MSKCC's corroborating mention is a single unelaborated sentence.

citations.label: NCCIH: Licorice Root
MSKCC: Licorice

claims.useCase: Adjunct to standard therapy for H. pylori-related peptic ulcer disease, including deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) specifically
claims.gradeRationale: A 2021 comprehensive review reports licorice added to standard triple therapy with clarithromycin improved H. pylori eradication rates (83.3% vs. 62.5% in the control group), though this figure traces only to the review's own summary and not an independently verified primary trial. The same review separately reports a placebo-controlled trial of deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) specifically for gastric ulcer healing found no difference in ulcer area after four weeks - an important nuance, since DGL is commonly marketed as a gentler alternative but was not shown to preserve ulcer-healing benefit in that trial. Left ungraded given the mixed within-use-case evidence and the unverified primary-source trace on the positive figure.

claims.useCase: Cough, sore throat, and postoperative sore-throat gargle
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states licorice gargle or lozenges used before surgery might lessen the severity of sore throat following intubation, and a 2021 review cites an older finding that licorice gargling halved the incidence of sore throat. But the newest and most rigorous trial found in this area - a 2024 randomized, double-blind trial of 127 postoperative patients - found licorice gargle produced no meaningful pain relief or reduced morphine use versus a sugar-water control. Left ungraded given this direct tension between NCCIH's framing and the newest dedicated RCT; the broader traditional use for cough and bronchitis is presented as historical use only, since no controlled-trial evidence specific to cough itself (as opposed to postoperative sore throat) was found.

A 2025 dermatology review independently corroborates this with five separately named small randomized trials (26-55 participants each) of licorice-derived topical preparations, most finding effects comparable to (non-inferior to) low- or mid-potency topical corticosteroids on symptom severity, relapse rate, or skin-barrier measures. This is the best-corroborated efficacy use case found for this herb, but every trial is small, several use non-inferiority designs against an active comparator rather than a placebo, the review's own authors describe the evidence as outdated with a lack of recent trials, and preparation terminology (whole licorice extract vs. the purified compound licochalcone A) is used inconsistently across the cited studies.

safetyNotes.text: Licorice's active compound glycyrrhizin can, in high doses or with prolonged use, cause a syndrome of water retention, low potassium (hypokalemia), and high blood pressure, and in severe cases cardiac rhythm disturbances or cardiac arrest. NCCIH and MSKCC both document this independently, and MSKCC's mechanism explanation traces it to glycyrrhizin blocking the enzyme that normally converts cortisol to cortisone, amplifying cortisol's blood-pressure- and potassium-lowering effects. A 2026 narrative review gives concrete thresholds: regulatory guidance flags formulations above 2.5 g of licorice per day, a newer database study found effects reported at doses as low as 1.125 g per day, and long-term use beyond 30 days is an independent risk factor, with older age, low body weight, concurrent diuretics or corticosteroids, and low blood albumin increasing risk further. A separate 2026 case-report analysis of glycyrrhiza-containing products documented real cases of hypokalemia, hypertension, arrhythmia, and one case of Torsades de Pointes (a dangerous heart rhythm). The EMA/HMPC monograph corroborates this independently, describing overdose cases after more than 4 weeks of use or high intake, with water retention, hypokalaemia, hypertension, cardiac rhythm disorders, and hypertensive encephalopathy.

NCCIH states that consuming about 250 grams of licorice per week during pregnancy is unsafe and can raise the risk of delivery before 38 weeks gestation; MSKCC corroborates an association between heavy licorice use and early preterm birth, citing a systematic review. A Finnish cohort study of children born to mothers with high glycyrrhizin exposure during pregnancy (defined at or above 500 mg of glycyrrhizin per week - a different unit than NCCIH's whole-product figure, not directly comparable) found differences in pubertal timing, body composition, and behavioral outcomes at around age 12; this study's exact effect sizes were not independently re-verified this session and should be confirmed before being quoted precisely. The EMA/HMPC monograph separately reports animal studies showing embryotoxicity and reproductive-toxicity signals and states use is not recommended during pregnancy, in women of childbearing potential not using contraception, or while breastfeeding.

Licorice has a wide range of documented and theoretical drug interactions. MSKCC describes potentiated toxicity risk with cardiac glycosides such as digoxin, increased hypokalemia risk with diuretics (independently corroborated by a 2026 case-report review, which also recommends regular monitoring of potassium, blood pressure, and creatine kinase during use), increased insulin sensitivity, reduced warfarin effectiveness via faster drug clearance (the opposite direction of concern from herbs that increase bleeding risk), reduced cyclosporine bioavailability, increased cortisol availability relevant to corticosteroid therapy (independently corroborated by NCCIH in general terms), reduced metformin effectiveness in an animal model only, interference with antihypertensive medications, potentiation of MAO inhibitor activity, induction of the CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 liver enzymes relevant to many other medications, and increased absorption of the chemotherapy drug daunorubicin. The EMA/HMPC monograph independently corroborates the diuretic, cardiac glycoside, corticosteroid, and CYP3A4 cautions, and states licorice may counteract prescribed antihypertensive medication; it specifically notes 300 mg/day of glycyrrhizin for 14 days modestly decreased exposure to CYP3A4-metabolized drugs such as midazolam and omeprazole in clinical studies. Anyone on these medication classes should talk with a healthcare provider before using licorice.

Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) has the glycyrrhizin removed specifically to reduce the blood-pressure and potassium risks above, and NCCIH states DGL might be safe for up to 4 months - the only specific duration-of-use figure NCCIH gives for any licorice preparation. MSKCC corroborates that researchers commonly use glycyrrhizin-free DGL extract specifically because of whole licorice's adverse-reaction profile. However, DGL's safety advantage does not automatically carry over to efficacy: a placebo-controlled trial of DGL for gastric ulcer healing found no measurable difference in ulcer area after four weeks (see the peptic-ulcer claim above), so DGL should not be assumed to retain whole licorice's traditional benefits.

As with other herbal dietary supplements, licorice products are not tested or approved by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale, so actual glycyrrhizin content can vary meaningfully between products and may not match label claims - a particular concern given how dose-dependent licorice's safety risks are.

name: Milk Thistle
summary: A spiny, purple-flowered thistle whose seeds yield silymarin, a mixture of plant compounds long used traditionally for liver disorders and now most studied as an oral supplement explored for liver health alongside conventional care, and — in a specific hospital-administered intravenous form — as part of emergency medical treatment for death-cap and other amatoxin mushroom poisoning; despite widespread popularity, NCCIH describes the human evidence for most liver-disease uses as inconclusive.

claims.useCase: Liver health support in chronic liver disease (hepatitis B/C, alcohol-related liver disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease/NASH, or chemotherapy- or toxin-related liver enzyme elevation), taken as an oral silymarin/milk thistle supplement alongside conventional medical care
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states there isn't enough high-quality evidence to draw firm conclusions about milk thistle's effects on liver-related health conditions, describing trial results for alcohol-related liver disease, hepatitis B and C, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and chemotherapy- or toxin-related liver damage as conflicting or too limited to support conclusions. Two NCCIH/NIDDK-funded randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials illustrate this directly: a 154-person, multicenter trial in people with chronic hepatitis C who had not responded to interferon-based therapy found that higher-than-customary doses of silymarin (420 mg or 700 mg, three times daily for 24 weeks) produced no significant difference from placebo in liver enzyme (ALT) response rates (about 4% in every arm), viral load, or quality of life. A separate 78-person trial in non-cirrhotic NASH patients (420 mg or 700 mg silymarin, three times daily for 48 weeks) found no significant difference from placebo on the primary histological improvement endpoint, and the authors described the overall effect of silymarin in NASH as inconclusive, calling for further trials. Left ungraded: despite a long traditional history of use for liver disorders and wide current marketing for this purpose, the best-available placebo-controlled human trials for these specific liver-disease uses have not shown a benefit over placebo, and NCCIH's own framing across the broader category remains explicitly inconclusive rather than clearly positive or negative. Milk thistle is not a substitute for a physician's ongoing management of any liver condition.

claims.useCase: Hospital-administered intravenous silibinin (a concentrated pharmaceutical-grade extract, brand name Legalon SIL) as part of emergency medical treatment for Amanita phalloides (death cap) and other amatoxin-containing mushroom poisoning
claims.gradeRationale: Randomized controlled trials of IV silibinin for amatoxin poisoning have not been conducted; a 2012 review states Phase III RCTs are not feasible given how rare and severe confirmed cases are. Instead, the evidence base is decades of consistent open-label and observational case-series data: a pooled retrospective analysis covering 1,491 documented Amanita-poisoned patients treated with Legalon SIL across North American and European centers found a 93% survival rate, with overall mortality under 10% compared with over 20% in historical cohorts managed with penicillin alone; that same review's summary table lists a foundational 1983 Austrian case series (Hruby et al.) of 15 patients, 14 of whom survived, with silibinin started up to 48 hours after ingestion still associated with less severe liver injury. Post-marketing safety surveillance of roughly 9,000 treated patients found no serious adverse drug reactions attributed to silibinin itself. IV silibinin is licensed specifically for this indication in more than a dozen European countries and, in the US, remains available only via case-by-case FDA Emergency Investigational New Drug authorization. Graded B per this app's rubric: multiple large, consistent human observational/case-series datasets rather than a randomized trial. Important distinction: this describes a hospital-administered IV pharmaceutical drug for a life-threatening emergency, not oral milk thistle supplement use — it is included here as context only, not as guidance to self-manage suspected mushroom poisoning, which requires immediate emergency care.

claims.useCase: Blood sugar (glycemic) support in type 2 diabetes, as an oral supplement adjunct
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH notes a small number of studies suggest milk thistle extracts may help control blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes, while cautioning that most of this research originates from a narrow set of countries, raising questions about how well it would generalize elsewhere. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 randomized controlled trials (270 patients total) found silymarin was associated with a statistically significant reduction in fasting blood glucose (-26.86 mg/dL) and HbA1c (-1.07 percentage points) compared with control, with no significant effect on lipid profile. However, the same review explicitly describes the underlying evidence as low-to-very-low quality, cites substantial heterogeneity between the included trials (differing doses, unclear randomization procedures, funding conflicts in some studies), and states plainly that despite the statistically significant pooled result, 'no recommendation can be made' without further, higher-quality trials. A separate, more recent meta-analysis was identified in search results as reporting broadly similar glucose- and LDL-lowering findings across 7 trials, but that paper sits behind a paywall and its findings were not independently verified for this entry. Graded C: a consistent, statistically significant direction of effect on blood glucose across independent trials, but not high confidence, given the trial quality, size, and heterogeneity concerns the reviewers themselves raise.

PMC: Silymarin in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials (Voroneanu et al., 2016)

safetyNotes.text: Milk thistle may cause allergic reactions, particularly in people allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, daisies, or other plants in the same (Asteraceae/Compositae) family; a government-run drugs-in-lactation database also notes rare reports of severe allergy and anaphylaxis. Avoid milk thistle if you have a known allergy to these plants.

Oral milk thistle is generally well tolerated. NCCIH reports the most common side effects are mild digestive symptoms — bloating, nausea, and gas — and other sources describe occasional diarrhea or loose stools as well.

A pharmacology review of human studies found milk thistle/silymarin has a low overall risk of clinically significant drug interactions, with probe-drug studies showing limited effect on several major liver enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP3A4) — including one trial finding no meaningful change in levels of the statin rosuvastatin, and others finding no meaningful change in the chemotherapy drug irinotecan. Evidence on the HIV medication indinavir is more mixed: one study found milk thistle reduced indinavir trough levels by about 25% and overall drug exposure by about 9%, though the study authors judged this reduction small enough that milk thistle 'should not interfere with indinavir therapy,' while a separate study found no significant effect on indinavir levels at all. The same pharmacology review flags two further specific exceptions worth attention: laboratory data suggest silybin can inhibit the CYP2C9 enzyme involved in warfarin metabolism (not yet confirmed in a clinical trial), and one small human study found milk thistle modestly increased blood levels of the transporter-dependent drug talinolol. Anyone taking warfarin or other CYP2C9- or P-glycoprotein-affected medications should talk with a healthcare provider before combining them with milk thistle.

Because milk thistle has shown blood-sugar-lowering effects in clinical trials of people with type 2 diabetes, combining it with diabetes medications (especially insulin or sulfonylureas) could theoretically add to their effect and raise the risk of low blood sugar. Anyone taking diabetes medication should monitor blood sugar closely and talk with a healthcare provider before adding milk thistle.

NCCIH states it isn't known whether milk thistle is safe to use during pregnancy. Breastfeeding data are more limited but somewhat reassuring: a government-run drugs-in-lactation database reports silymarin's components are largely undetectable in breastmilk and considered poorly absorbed by infants, and studies of breastfeeding infants of mothers taking it found no adverse effects, though no direct infant blood-level data exist. Evidence that milk thistle increases milk supply is mixed across trials and rated low-certainty by a systematic review, and should not replace evaluation of other factors affecting milk production. Talk with a healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

Milk thistle supplements have not shown a meaningful benefit over placebo in the largest controlled trials for hepatitis C or NASH (see claims above) and should not replace a physician's ongoing monitoring and management of hepatitis, cirrhosis, or other liver disease.

Suspected poisoning by Amanita phalloides (death cap) or other amatoxin-containing mushrooms is a medical emergency. Oral milk thistle supplements are not equivalent to, and should not be used in place of, the specific intravenous pharmaceutical-grade silibinin formulation administered in hospitals for this indication — call Poison Control or emergency services immediately if mushroom poisoning is suspected.

As a dietary supplement, milk thistle is not tested by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale; NCCIH notes some products have been found to contain silymarin levels substantially different from what's stated on the label, and others have been contaminated with pesticides, microorganisms, or mycotoxins.

name: Passionflower
summary: A climbing vine native to the southeastern U.S. and Central/South America, long used as a traditional sedative and now studied mainly as a short-term oral supplement for anxiety, including generalized anxiety and anxiety before surgical or dental procedures, where several small trials found effects comparable to low-dose benzodiazepines. With much thinner, single-study evidence, it is also studied for sleep quality, ADHD symptoms, and as an adjunct to ease benzodiazepine tapering or opiate withdrawal. It is generally well tolerated but carries a real sedative-interaction caution with other CNS depressants and a pregnancy contraindication due to a possible uterine-stimulant effect.

claims.useCase: Anxiety (generalized anxiety and pre-surgical/pre-dental anxiety)
claims.gradeRationale: Genuinely contested evidence, best represented honestly rather than flattened. A 2020 systematic review of nine RCTs (published 2008-2019) found consistently positive individual trial results, including several head-to-head trials against real benzodiazepine comparators (oxazepam, midazolam) showing comparable anxiety reduction, with no adverse effects observed and one trial suggesting a functional-impairment advantage over oxazepam. However, the only formal Cochrane review on this question (2007, pooling just 2 studies/198 participants, never updated since) concluded available trials were insufficient in number 'to permit any conclusions to be drawn.' A separate 2013 ethnopharmacology review directly criticized the methodological rigor of this same trial literature (poor extract-ratio reporting, limited samples, weak blinding/randomization documentation, incorrect placebo definitions) while affirming the plant's safety profile. All individual trials are small (n=30-128), mostly single-country (5 of 9 in Iran), and a formal meta-analysis has never been feasible due to heterogeneity. Left ungraded given this genuine three-way tension between a newer positive-leaning trial base, an unresuperseded Cochrane 'insufficient evidence' verdict, and a direct methodological critique of the same literature.

claims.gradeRationale: This is the thinnest of passionflower's commonly marketed uses, resting on a single identified RCT (n=41, 22 days, passionflower tea vs. placebo tea) that found a significant but modest improvement in a subjective sleep-quality measure (mean increase 5.2%). Left ungraded given the single-trial, non-replicated status.

claims.useCase: ADHD (adjunct/alternative support)
claims.gradeRationale: The weakest-evidenced use case researched. NCCIH states there is not enough evidence to say whether passionflower is helpful for ADHD. An independent systematic review of herbal medicines for pediatric ADHD (9 RCTs, 464 patients, across 7 herbs) rated Passiflora-specific evidence 'low,' grouped with (not distinguished from) valerian and lemon balm, concluding no concrete recommendations for use can be made. A separate small pediatric trial mentioned by a secondary source as showing benefit comparable to a prescription drug could not be independently located or verified in the underlying literature search. Left ungraded and presented as insufficient evidence.

claims.useCase: Benzodiazepine tapering support (adjunct)
claims.gradeRationale: The most recent and, by sample size, largest evidence found for passionflower, but observational rather than randomized. A 2026 retrospective study (n=186) found adjunctive passionflower significantly reduced benzodiazepine dosage at 3 months versus baseline (p<0.001), with a dose-response signal favoring 400-600mg/day over 200mg/day, alongside a smaller 2024 study from the same research group reporting sustained benefit with no rebound or withdrawal effect on discontinuation. Both studies are retrospective/observational (not randomized), come from the same research group with likely overlapping patient populations, and the authors themselves state prospective controlled trials are still needed. Left ungraded given the lack of randomization and independent replication, despite the statistically significant, real-world signal.

claims.useCase: Opiate withdrawal support (adjunct to clonidine)
claims.gradeRationale: A single small RCT (n=65 opiate-dependent outpatients, 14 days) found passiflora added to clonidine was significantly superior to clonidine alone for the psychological/mental symptoms of withdrawal, though both arms were equally effective for physical withdrawal symptoms. The trial authors themselves noted a larger confirmatory study was warranted. No human replication was located; the only adjacent supporting data is a mouse study on a Passiflora-based product attenuating morphine withdrawal, which is preclinical mechanistic support, not human clinical corroboration. Left ungraded given the single-trial, non-replicated status.

safetyNotes.text: Sedative/CNS-depressant interaction, including benzodiazepines (clonazepam, lorazepam), barbiturates (pentobarbital, phenobarbital, secobarbital), and zolpidem, with a concern for additive drowsiness/CNS depression. A consumer drug-interaction reference rates this interaction 'Moderate,' but a documented case report describes a patient combining valerian and passionflower with lorazepam who experienced hand tremors, dizziness, and muscular fatigue, with an additive or synergistic effect suspected by the reporting clinicians - the elevated severity here reflects that case report rather than the reference sources' own moderate rating. No source specifically named alcohol as an interacting substance for passionflower; the general sedative-interaction mechanism should be assumed to extend to other CNS depressants including alcohol.

Drowsiness, dizziness, and confusion are common, well-corroborated side effects across three independent sources, along with lack of muscle coordination and impaired cognitive function in some users. Generally described as mild and consistent with the herb's sedative mechanism.

Not recommended during pregnancy: passionflower may induce uterine contractions and, per animal data, has been associated with behavioral disruption in offspring. Safety during breastfeeding is not well established. Corroborated independently across three sources.

Large doses may cause central nervous system depression and irregular heart rhythms, including bradycardia, prolonged QTc, and ventricular tachycardia. A documented case describes a 34-year-old woman hospitalized with nausea, vomiting, decreased heart rate, and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia with QTc prolongation after using a passionflower-containing supplement. This is a single case-report-level finding not corroborated by a second independent source for the cardiac-specific mechanism.

Possible additive interaction with other QT-prolonging drugs (examples cited: azithromycin, dasatinib, fingolimod) for potential added cardiac effects. Single-sourced, and the source itself states clinical significance is not known.
May enhance the potency of St. John's wort. Single-sourced, with clinical significance stated as not known by the source itself.

May interact with anesthesia and other perioperative medications, potentially slowing the nervous system too much; recommended to stop use at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery. Corroborated independently across two sources, consistent on both mechanism and timing.

Liver safety is reassuring and well-corroborated: the NIH's LiverTox database assigns passionflower Likelihood Category E ('unlikely cause of clinically apparent liver injury'), with no convincing case reports linking it to clinically apparent liver injury. A 2014 study of 85 herbal/supplement-related liver-injury cases found passionflower was not implicated in any of them, and several independent hepatotoxicity reviews do not list it at all among supplement-related liver-injury causes. This is a notably more reassuring picture than some other sedative herbs' liver-safety ratings in this glossary.

As a dietary supplement, passionflower is not pre-approved by the FDA for safety or efficacy before sale; large amounts (e.g., roughly 3.5 grams of a specific extract over a 2-day period) are rated possibly unsafe, underscoring that dose and product-quality control are not standardized.

Drug-interaction data for passionflower overall is thin: most named interactions across available sources are explicitly hedged by the sources themselves as being of unknown clinical relevance, or are based on general mechanism rather than reported clinical cases at scale. Only the sedative/CNS-depressant interaction and the anesthesia/perioperative caution have two-source corroboration.

name: Peppermint
summary: A cooling, menthol-rich mint hybrid whose enteric-coated oil is among the more studied natural options for irritable bowel syndrome symptoms, alongside long traditional tea use for occasional digestive discomfort.

claims.useCase: Occasional indigestion, gas, and digestive discomfort
claims.gradeRationale: Peppermint has a long traditional history for digestive complaints. NCCIH notes peppermint tea appears safe and that combination products containing peppermint oil plus caraway oil may help with indigestion, but states there is very little dedicated research on peppermint leaf/tea itself (most trial evidence is on peppermint oil for IBS specifically). Left ungraded pending herb-leaf-specific evidence.

safetyNotes.text: Oral peppermint oil can cause heartburn, indigestion-type discomfort, abdominal pain, or dry mouth in some people; enteric-coated capsules are often used specifically to reduce the likelihood of heartburn.
Rare allergic reactions to peppermint oil have been reported; topical use can occasionally cause skin rash or irritation.
Peppermint oil (and its menthol content) should never be applied to the face of infants or young children — serious side effects can occur if inhaled.

Peppermint in ordinary food amounts appears safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but little is known about the safety of medicinal-strength oral peppermint oil in pregnancy or while breastfeeding; if used on the nipples for breastfeeding comfort it should be wiped off before the next feed so the infant does not inhale menthol.
No specific, well-documented drug interactions were found for peppermint; as with any herbal product, talk to a healthcare provider before use if you take prescription medication.

name: Rhodiola
summary: A high-altitude root long used in Russian, Scandinavian, and other traditional medicine, now widely sold as an 'adaptogen' supplement marketed for stress, fatigue, athletic performance, and mood. A body of small, short, and methodologically inconsistent randomized trials points in a generally positive direction for physical/mental fatigue and endurance exercise, but NCCIH itself and an independent expert psychiatric taskforce both describe the overall evidence, especially for depression and mood, as too weak or unsupportive to draw firm conclusions from. Rhodiola is also one of the more commonly adulterated botanical supplements on the market, a real product-quality concern independent of the efficacy question.

claims.useCase: Stress and physical/mental fatigue ('adaptogen' claim)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH's own framing is unusually blunt: 'there isn't enough reliable evidence to determine whether rhodiola or its components are useful for any health-related purpose,' and 'most of the research in people is of low-to-moderate quality.' The most directly relevant systematic review (11 trials, 446 total subjects) found only 2 of 6 physical-fatigue studies and 3 of 5 mental-fatigue studies showed a significant positive effect, several with methodological caveats (unvalidated outcome measures, unexplained participant exclusions), and concluded in its own words that 'the current evidence for efficacy of R. rosea is contradictory and inconclusive.' Marketing claims that rhodiola normalizes stress hormones via the HPA axis are also not clearly supported: a 2022 systematic review of plants and the HPA axis singled out ashwagandha, not rhodiola, as the one substance with a reasonably reliable cortisol effect. Left ungraded given the reviewing authors' own 'contradictory and inconclusive' verdict; adverse events across the fatigue trials were reassuringly few and mild.

Ishaque et al., "Rhodiola rosea for physical and mental fatigue: a systematic review," BMC Complement Altern Med, 2012
Lopresti, Smith & Drummond, "Modulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis by plants and phytonutrients: a systematic review of human trials," Nutritional Neuroscience, 2022

claims.useCase: Physical/athletic performance under exertion (endurance and anaerobic performance, exercise-induced muscle damage)
claims.gradeRationale: The most consistent, largest, and most recent positive trial signal found for rhodiola. A 2025 meta-analysis pooling 26 RCTs (668 participants) found significant improvements in VO2max (low heterogeneity, 11 studies), time to exhaustion, and time-trial performance, alongside favorable changes in oxidative-stress and muscle-damage biomarkers, and concluded the evidence 'provides strong evidence supporting the positive effects' of rhodiola on endurance. However, quality was assessed with the PEDro scale rather than GRADE or Cochrane risk-of-bias tools, only one outcome (VO2max) had more than 10 pooled studies, and inflammatory-marker results were inconclusive with very high heterogeneity. A second, smaller 2023 review analyzing the same broad literature by acute-vs-chronic dosing found a different pattern: chronic supplementation helped anaerobic performance and muscle-damage markers but not endurance performance specifically, while acute supplementation helped endurance. Graded C to reflect a real, comparatively well-powered positive signal that nonetheless rests on non-GRADE quality assessment, a young/recreational-athlete-dominated population, and a genuine acute-vs-chronic nuance the two best reviews handle differently.

Wang, Yang, Gao, Zeng & Liu, "The effect of Rhodiola rosea supplementation on endurance performance and related biomarkers: a systematic review and meta-analysis," Front Nutr, 2025
Sanz-Barrio et al., "Rhodiola rosea supplementation on sports performance: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials," Phytother Res, 2023

claims.useCase: Mild-to-moderate depression
claims.gradeRationale: A genuinely split evidence picture. One placebo-controlled trial found significant improvement in depressive symptoms, insomnia, and emotional instability at two rhodiola doses versus placebo. A second, 3-arm proof-of-concept trial found rhodiola produced only a modest, statistically non-significant reduction in depression scores versus placebo, with the authors framing rhodiola's appeal as better tolerability rather than superior efficacy versus sertraline. A third trial found rhodiola added to sertraline outperformed sertraline alone, but this is evidence for rhodiola as an adjunct, not as standalone treatment. Weighing against the positive individual trials, a 2022 expert clinician guideline from a 31-expert, 15-country psychiatric taskforce (the same one NCCIH itself references) explicitly states 'rhodiola use was not supported for use in mood disorders,' in contrast to St. John's wort and saffron, which received positive recommendations in the same guideline. Left ungraded given this direct conflict between small positive trials and an authoritative guideline-level non-recommendation.

safetyNotes.text: CYP2C9 enzyme inhibition, with a real interaction risk for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs including warfarin and phenytoin. A randomized human trial (13 healthy volunteers) found rhodiola pretreatment significantly reduced CYP2C9 enzyme activity, corroborated by an in vitro study from the same research group showing direct CYP2C9 inhibition, and by an earlier animal study finding rhodiola co-administration roughly doubled losartan's blood levels. The authors' own conclusion is that this effect might be clinically relevant during treatment with CYP2C9 substrates with a narrow therapeutic index, specifically naming phenytoin and warfarin.

Monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitory activity, which could increase serotonergic side effects when combined with antidepressants and could amplify effects when combined with other stimulant or serotonergic drugs, though clinical significance is not yet confirmed in humans generally. A cited case report describes a 26-year-old woman who developed a fast, irregular heartbeat after taking rhodiola alongside her prescribed antidepressant for three days. A consumer drug-interaction reference separately rates a rhodiola-escitalopram interaction 'Moderate.' No source found names caffeine specifically as an interacting substance; any caffeine-related caution rests on mechanistic inference (MAO-inhibitory plus stimulant-like properties), not a directly documented interaction.

Possible additive effect with diabetes/blood-sugar-lowering medications (examples: glimepiride, glyburide, insulin, pioglitazone, rosiglitazone), rated 'Moderate' by a consumer drug-interaction reference. No human trial evidence of a rhodiola blood-glucose-lowering effect was found; the underlying signal comes only from animal/preclinical studies, so this caution rests on a lower evidence tier than the CYP2C9/warfarin note above.

Possible additive effect with blood-pressure-lowering medications (examples: captopril, enalapril, losartan, valsartan, diltiazem, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide), rated 'Moderate' by a consumer drug-interaction reference. This is currently single-sourced, with no independent corroboration found from NCCIH or MSKCC.

A theoretical mania-triggering risk in bipolar disorder is sometimes raised for stimulating adaptogens generally, but no source (NCCIH, MSKCC, a consumer drug-interaction reference, or a targeted literature search) was found documenting this specifically for rhodiola. Rhodiola's documented MAO-inhibitory and stimulant-like properties make such a risk mechanistically plausible by analogy to other stimulating compounds, but this is not an established, source-confirmed risk and should be presented as a theoretical caution only.

Generally well tolerated short-term, with possible side effects including dizziness, headache, insomnia, and either dry mouth or excessive saliva production. NCCIH describes rhodiola as possibly safe for up to 12 weeks; a consumer reference cites a shorter 6-10 week window. Across the largest fatigue-trial systematic review (446 subjects, 11 trials), only 5 adverse events were reported, mostly mild, several occurring in placebo arms. No source found establishes safety for continuous, multi-month-to-year use, and this data gap should be stated plainly.

Not recommended during pregnancy or while breastfeeding due to insufficient safety data. NCCIH frames this neutrally as 'little is known,' while a consumer reference more directly recommends avoidance during both pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Product-quality and adulteration concerns are well-corroborated across four independent peer-reviewed analytical-chemistry studies (DNA barcoding, NMR/HPLC, HPTLC, and effect-directed chromatography) on products from different markets, all finding that a substantial share of commercial rhodiola products tested did not contain the labeled species, the labeled marker-compound content, or both — including some products substituted with fenugreek, alfalfa, or a different Rhodiola species entirely. Recommend choosing a reputable, third-party-tested source.

No dedicated NIH LiverTox monograph currently exists for rhodiola (confirmed via direct index check, not just a failed URL guess). This is an absence-of-evidence finding, not a documented reassurance of liver safety.
As a dietary supplement, rhodiola is not pre-approved by the FDA for safety or efficacy before sale.

May stimulate immune activity, which could theoretically counteract immunosuppressant drugs including azathioprine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and corticosteroids, rated 'Moderate' by a consumer drug-interaction reference. This is currently single-sourced, with no independent corroboration found from NCCIH or MSKCC.

name: Saw Palmetto
summary: A small palm whose berries are widely sold as a supplement for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms; the evidence story has genuinely evolved over two decades from encouraging small early trials to a now well-established negative finding in large, high-quality research, with two major NIH-funded trials and a high-certainty 2023 Cochrane review all concluding saw palmetto alone provides little to no benefit for urinary symptoms. Combination products pairing it with other herbs show a more promising but still uncertain, low-certainty signal.

claims.useCase: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and lower urinary tract symptoms, saw palmetto used alone
claims.gradeRationale: Saw palmetto is one of the most rigorously tested single-herb interventions in this glossary, and the evidence has evolved from early positive-leaning small and often industry-funded trials to a now-settled negative finding in large, high-quality research. The NIH-funded CAMUS trial (Barry et al., JAMA 2011; 369 men, 72 weeks, doses escalating from the standard 320 mg/day up to 960 mg/day) found saw palmetto extract produced less symptom improvement than placebo on its primary outcome (a 2.20-point improvement versus a 2.99-point improvement with placebo, not significant), with no significant benefit on any secondary outcome including peak urinary flow, PSA, or quality of life. This followed an earlier single-institution trial (the STEP trial) that found no benefit at the standard dose. The 2023 Cochrane systematic review (Franco et al.; 19 placebo-controlled monotherapy trials, part of a larger 27-study, 4,656-participant review) rated its findings high-certainty evidence and concluded 'Serenoa repens alone provides little to no benefit for men with LUTS,' with both short-term and long-term pooled symptom-score results falling below any plausible threshold for clinical meaningfulness despite occasional statistical significance. NCCIH's current position matches this: 'we know enough to conclude saw palmetto is probably not helpful for this purpose.' Graded F: this is not an absence of evidence but multiple large, well-designed, placebo-controlled trials, corroborated by an independent high-certainty systematic review, that specifically tested for and did not find a benefit.

claims.useCase: BPH and lower urinary tract symptoms, saw palmetto combined with other herbs (such as nettle root or pygeum-containing blends)
claims.gradeRationale: Unlike monotherapy, where the evidence is now settled-negative, the 2023 Cochrane review frames combination phytotherapy as a genuinely open question. Pooling 4 trials with 460 participants of Serenoa repens combined with another herb versus placebo found a larger apparent symptom benefit (IPSS mean difference -2.41) but rated only low-certainty evidence, downgraded for substantial inconsistency between trials; quality-of-life results across these same trials were rated very-low-certainty and were highly inconsistent between individual trials. NCCIH's own framing describes combination-herb evidence as 'inconclusive.' A specific, frequently cited saw palmetto plus stinging nettle root product trial comparing it against the drug tamsulosin could not be independently verified from a primary source during this research and its specific numbers should not be relied on. Left ungraded: real trial-level signal exists for combination products, but the review authors themselves call it uncertain rather than established.

claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states evidence for saw palmetto and hair loss is 'too limited to allow conclusions to be reached.' A systematic review pooling 7 studies of oral or topical saw palmetto for androgenetic alopecia and telogen effluvium reported positive numeric findings on hair quality, hair count, and density with no serious adverse events, but the review's own authors state 'robust high-quality data are lacking' and call for further large-scale trials isolating saw palmetto's own contribution before it can be confirmed effective. Individual trials in this space are small, short, and frequently combine saw palmetto with other active ingredients like pumpkin seed oil or biotin, making it hard to isolate saw palmetto's independent effect. A widely cited comparative study reportedly found saw palmetto produced meaningfully less hair improvement than the drug finasteride, but this could not be independently verified from a primary source. Left ungraded: a real, growing, but still preliminary and low-quality body of small trials with a mix of formulations and no established standard dose.

safetyNotes.text: Saw palmetto is generally well tolerated. NCCIH describes it as safely used in research studies for up to 3 years, with mild and infrequent adverse effects including digestive symptoms, dizziness, and headache; a consumer drug-interaction reference notes these side effects do not seem to occur more often than with a placebo. Decreased libido and rhinitis have also been reported as mild effects.

Saw palmetto's effect on bleeding is a genuinely debated safety question, not a settled one. Case reports have raised concern about prolonged bleeding time and additive anticoagulant effects, and reputable sources advise against combining saw palmetto with warfarin, other blood thinners, or antiplatelet medications like clopidogrel or NSAIDs, with a common recommendation to stop use at least 2 weeks before scheduled surgery. However, some more recent controlled evidence has not confirmed a strong bleeding-risk effect. Given this unresolved tension, the more conservative stance (avoid combining with blood thinners, stop before surgery) is the safer one to follow, and anyone on blood-thinning medication or facing surgery should talk with a healthcare provider.

Saw palmetto is understood to reduce testosterone and DHT levels by inhibiting the same enzyme (5-alpha-reductase) targeted by the drug finasteride. It may decrease the effectiveness of birth control pills and estrogen medications, so backup contraception and provider consultation are recommended when combining them. Case reports describe hormonal disruption, including hot flashes and early menarche, in children given saw palmetto for hair-related conditions.

Saw palmetto does not appear to affect PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, even at higher-than-usual doses, a finding corroborated by NCCIH, the CAMUS trial, and MSKCC. This is reassuring in one specific respect: saw palmetto is not expected to mask a PSA level that might otherwise prompt further prostate-cancer evaluation.

Rare, self-limited liver injury has been reported with saw palmetto. NIH's LiverTox database gives it a Likelihood Score of D, a possible but rare cause of clinically apparent liver injury, based on a small number of case reports of jaundice or acute liver injury with onset 1-2 weeks after starting, resolving within 1-3 months with no reported cases leading to death, transplantation, or chronic liver disease.

Saw palmetto may be unsafe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding, likely related to its hormonal activity; this caution is independently corroborated by NCCIH and a consumer drug-interaction reference.

New or worsening urinary symptoms should be evaluated by a healthcare provider before self-treating with any supplement, since such symptoms can occasionally signal a more serious underlying condition; standard evaluation may include PSA testing. Note that BPH itself is not cancer and does not increase prostate cancer risk.

name: Turmeric
summary: A bright yellow rhizome long used in South and Southeast Asian cooking and traditional medicine, most studied today as an oral curcumin/turmeric extract supplement for joint comfort, alongside long traditional use for occasional digestive discomfort.

claims.useCase: Knee osteoarthritis joint discomfort and function (oral curcumin/turmeric extract supplements)
claims.gradeRationale: A 2025 umbrella review of ten systematic reviews and meta-analyses found curcumin formulations produced statistically significant improvements in pain (VAS) and function/stiffness (WOMAC) versus comparators in knee osteoarthritis, with efficacy signals described as comparable to NSAIDs and a more favorable tolerability profile in the available trials. However, the same review rated most of the underlying evidence as low to very-low quality with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 99%) and incomplete safety reporting, and NCCIH's own overview states there isn't yet enough evidence to definitively conclude that oral or topical turmeric/curcumin is beneficial for any health purpose, including knee osteoarthritis pain specifically. Graded C: a consistent positive direction of effect across many independent trials, but not high-confidence given the quality and heterogeneity concerns.

claims.useCase: Occasional indigestion or functional dyspepsia (oral turmeric or curcumin)
claims.gradeRationale: Findings across small randomized trials are mixed rather than consistently positive. An open-label randomized trial found Curcuma longa produced short-term symptom relief comparable to the over-the-counter comparator simethicone at 2 and 4 weeks without serious adverse events, but with a higher rate of symptom recurrence after stopping treatment. A separate 206-patient randomized trial reported comparable efficacy between curcumin and the proton-pump inhibitor omeprazole (with no added benefit from combining them), though satisfaction scores improved less over time in curcumin users and some liver-enzyme changes were noted among overweight participants taking curcumin. Neither trial found here compared curcumin against a placebo arm, so a placebo-beating effect specific to dyspepsia is not yet confirmed. Left ungraded pending clearer placebo-controlled evidence, despite turmeric's long traditional use for indigestion and abdominal complaints.

claims.useCase: General anti-inflammatory or overall-wellness supplement use
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states plainly that there isn't enough evidence to definitively conclude whether oral turmeric or curcumin has beneficial effects for the wide range of conditions it is marketed for, and notes it is hard to compare studies because oral curcumin products vary widely in how much curcumin they actually contain. Left ungraded: broad anti-inflammatory or general-wellness framing is not itself a specific, evidence-tested use case.

safetyNotes.text: Oral turmeric or curcumin can cause nausea, vomiting, acid reflux, stomach upset, diarrhea, or constipation in some people; topical curcumin can cause hives or itching.

High-bioavailability curcumin formulations (often combined with black pepper/piperine extract or lipid-based delivery to boost absorption) have been linked to a growing number of liver injury cases, including outbreaks of acute hepatitis. NIH's LiverTox database describes turmeric as having become the most common reported cause of clinically apparent herbal-related liver injury in the United States, typically appearing 1-4 months after starting use as fatigue, nausea, poor appetite, dark urine, or jaundice. Stop use and contact a healthcare provider promptly if these symptoms occur.

Curcumin increases bile secretion and gallbladder contraction. A published case report describes gallbladder perforation in a person with pre-existing gallstones after about 4 months of high-dose curcumin supplementation (1,500-2,000 mg/day); concentrated curcumin/turmeric supplements are considered inadvisable for people with gallstones or bile duct obstruction. This caution applies to concentrated supplements, not ordinary culinary turmeric use.

People with a personal or family history of kidney stones should talk to a healthcare provider before taking turmeric supplements; turmeric can raise urinary oxalate, and a case report links chronic high-dose turmeric use to oxalate nephropathy that improved after stopping.

Turmeric/curcumin may increase bleeding risk when combined with blood-thinning medications such as warfarin, aspirin, or other anticoagulants/antiplatelets. Case reports include a patient on previously stable warfarin whose INR rose above 10 within weeks of starting a turmeric product, and curcumin has documented antiplatelet and NSAID-like effects in the pharmacology literature. Talk to a healthcare provider before combining turmeric supplements with blood-thinning medication.

Animal research suggests curcumin can inhibit the intestinal enzyme (CYP3A4) that metabolizes some sulfonylurea diabetes medications (for example glibenclamide), prolonging their presence in the body; this could theoretically add to blood-sugar-lowering effects, though it has not been confirmed in human clinical trials. People taking diabetes medication should monitor blood sugar closely and talk to a healthcare provider before adding curcumin supplements.
NCCIH notes that use of turmeric supplements during pregnancy may be unsafe, and little is known about the safety of turmeric in amounts greater than typical food use while breastfeeding.

name: Valerian
summary: A flowering European and Asian plant whose dried root is one of the most widely used traditional sleep aids, marketed today as a supplement for insomnia, anxiety, and menopausal symptoms; despite decades of trials, the human evidence for its best-known use — helping people fall or stay asleep — remains genuinely and specifically contradicted by a formal sleep-medicine society guideline and by the most methodologically rigorous individual studies, even though it is consistently described as safe with only rare, mild adverse effects.

claims.useCase: Sleep/insomnia (oral root extract or tea)
claims.gradeRationale: Evidence here is a genuine, well-documented conflict rather than merely thin. NCCIH states research results on valerian for sleep problems are inconsistent, and that a 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) clinical practice guideline recommended against using valerian for chronic insomnia in adults; the guideline itself (Sateia et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2017) states verbatim, 'We suggest that clinicians not use valerian... in adults. (WEAK)' — a weak recommendation against use reflecting low-confidence evidence. The most commonly cited positive meta-analysis (Bent et al. 2006, Am J Med, 16 RCTs/1,093 patients) found a significant relative risk of 1.8 favoring valerian on a dichotomous 'improved sleep' measure, but a later, more careful systematic review (Taibi et al. 2007, Sleep Medicine Reviews, title: 'A systematic review of valerian as a sleep aid: Safe but not effective') directly critiques it by name for pooling combination products with up to eight other herbs and for a publication bias toward small, positive studies; Taibi's review of 37 studies concludes 'none of the most recent studies, which were also the most methodologically rigorous, found significant effects of valerian on sleep,' and that in 2 of the 6 trials driving Bent's own positive result, the actual sleep-quality ratings 'showed no significant differences between valerian and placebo.' Even the more sympathetic Fernández-San-Martín et al. 2010 meta-analysis (18 RCTs/1,317 participants) concluded valerian showed only subjective improvement, 'not... demonstrated with quantitative or objective measurements,' and flagged most included trials as poor quality. The most current synthesis available, a 2024 umbrella review (Valente et al., European Neuropsychopharmacology) that screened 70 records down to 8 qualifying systematic reviews, reaches the same conclusion: no evidence of efficacy for insomnia, with valerian appearing to help only subjectively-reported sleep quality, an effect 'not demonstrated with quantitative or objective measurements.' Left ungraded, matching this app's handling of hawthorn's similarly contradicted exercise-tolerance claim: a positive pooled signal exists in older individual trials, but it is specifically and directly disputed by a formal clinical guideline, the most rigorous individual trials, and the most recent, most comprehensive umbrella review of the evidence.

claims.useCase: Anxiety (oral root extract)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states there is not enough evidence to allow any conclusions about whether valerian is helpful for anxiety. The one anxiety-relevant randomized trial identified in this research (Jacobs, Bent, Tice et al. 2005, Medicine 84(4):197-207 — an internet-based RCT of valerian vs. kava vs. placebo in 391 people with sleep disturbance and anxiety or depression), as tabulated in the Taibi et al. 2007 systematic review, found insomnia-severity and subjective-sleep scores improved in all three arms, but improvement was greatest in the placebo group, with neither herbal treatment differing significantly from placebo. Left ungraded: no positive human trial evidence was identified, and NCCIH's own framing and the one located trial both point the same direction. This reflects traditional/promotional use rather than a tested clinical benefit.

claims.useCase: Menopausal symptoms (hot flashes, sleep disturbance during menopause)
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states three small studies suggest valerian might be helpful for menopause symptoms, but frames this as not enough evidence to know for certain. One of those studies, Jenabi et al. 2018 (Women & Health), was independently verified via adversarial fact-check: a triple-blind RCT of 60 postmenopausal women found valerian 530mg twice daily for 2 months produced a statistically significant reduction in hot-flash severity (p=.048 at 1 month, p=.020 at 2 months) and frequency (p=.033 at 2 months) versus placebo. This is a real, confirmed positive finding in one small trial, but remains within NCCIH's own 'not enough to know for certain' framing given the overall evidence is still just three small studies. Left ungraded: report as limited, small-study evidence suggesting possible benefit, not a firm conclusion.

claims.useCase: Traditional/historical use for digestive complaints, urinary complaints, and general nervous tension
claims.gradeRationale: NIH's LiverTox reference describes valerian as widely used in herbal medicine for insomnia, anxiety, and digestive and urinary problems, used for centuries in Europe primarily for digestive and urinary complaints. NCCIH separately notes valerian has been used medicinally since early Greece and Rome for insomnia, migraine, fatigue, and stomach cramps. Left ungraded: this reflects traditional and historical use only, without independently verified modern trial evidence for these specific complaints.

safetyNotes.text: Valerian has been associated with rare cases of liver injury. NIH's LiverTox database gives valerian a Likelihood Score of C — a probable rare cause of clinically apparent liver injury — describing reported hepatotoxicity as usually mild-to-moderate and self-limiting, with the underlying mechanism unknown. This is independently corroborated by the Taibi et al. 2007 systematic review, which notes valerian has been implicated in a few case reports of transient liver dysfunction, though no liver-related adverse events were reported within its own reviewed controlled-trial literature. This is a notably lower LiverTox score than black cohosh's (A, a well-established cause), but anyone with an existing liver condition should talk to a healthcare provider before use, and anyone taking valerian who develops abdominal pain, dark urine, or jaundice should stop use and seek care.

The most commonly reported side effects are mild: headache, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, and morning grogginess or a 'hangover' feeling, consistent across NCCIH, RxList, MSKCC, and trial data tabulated in the Taibi systematic review.

Valerian should not be combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedating medications (including barbiturates and certain pain or anesthesia medications), given a consistent risk of added drowsiness or over-sedation reported across NCCIH, RxList, the Taibi systematic review, and MSKCC. RxList rates the alcohol combination a 'Major' interaction to avoid.

Because of its sedative interaction potential, consumer references (MSKCC, RxList) advise stopping valerian before a scheduled surgery, though they disagree on the exact timing — MSKCC suggests at least 1 week, RxList suggests at least 2 weeks. Given this discrepancy and the lack of a primary anesthesiology source identified for this research, the more conservative window is worth following, and anyone with upcoming surgery should confirm timing with their surgical team.

Abruptly stopping valerian after regular, longer-term use may cause withdrawal-type symptoms, per consumer/professional reference sources (MSKCC, RxList), which recommend tapering the dose over a week or two rather than stopping suddenly. NCCIH separately notes the safety of long-term valerian use is unknown.

Laboratory research cited in the Taibi systematic review found mild to moderate in vitro inhibition of the CYP3A4 liver enzyme, but a human in vivo study (Gurley et al. 2005) found no significant effect of one valerian preparation on medications used to test enzyme activity, leading that review to conclude valerian is unlikely to significantly affect drug metabolism overall — while still advising caution with medications metabolized by CYP3A4 that have a narrow safety margin, such as digoxin.

Little is known about whether valerian is safe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. NCCIH and RxList both describe the safety data as insufficient and recommend avoiding use; MSKCC separately cites animal data showing reduced levels of essential micronutrients in fetal brain tissue with valerian exposure.

traditionalCombinations.note: Valerian and hops are a formally recognized traditional combination, not just an informal pairing — the European Medicines Agency's herbal-medicines committee (HMPC) maintains a joint assessment document for valerian root and hops flower as an established combination category. However, the largest and best-designed controlled trial of this combination (Morin et al. 2005, Sleep, 184 adults with mild insomnia) found only a modest, mostly non-significant benefit over placebo on sleep-continuity measures, and a systematic review of 6 controlled trials (Taibi et al. 2007) concluded combination products have not been shown to be more effective than valerian alone. Presented here as a traditionally and pharmacopoeially recognized pairing, not a proven-more-effective one.

traditionalCombinations.note: A commonly used traditional pairing with real trial history, though results are mixed. A systematic review (Taibi et al. 2007) tabulates 4 controlled trials: one (Dressing et al. 1996, n=49) found the combination significantly improved subjective sleep quality versus placebo, while two others found no significant difference from placebo on standardized sleep-quality scales. As with valerian-hops, this is presented as a traditional pairing with genuinely mixed controlled-trial support, not a well-established superior combination.

name: Witch Hazel
summary: A tannin-rich North American shrub whose steam-distilled bark/leaf water is a long-standing topical astringent, recognized by the FDA as an over-the-counter astringent ingredient for anorectal (hemorrhoidal) discomfort and used traditionally on minor skin irritation, insect bites, and small cuts; the best-controlled trial of witch hazel for mild atopic eczema found no meaningful benefit over an inactive vehicle, and evidence for acne-specific benefit remains preliminary, cell-culture-only research.

claims.useCase: Temporary relief of anorectal (hemorrhoidal) irritation and burning (topical astringent, external use)
claims.gradeRationale: Witch hazel is listed by the U.S. FDA as an approved astringent active ingredient (10-50%) for over-the-counter anorectal drug products under 21 CFR 346.18(b), and products meeting this monograph are permitted to state that they 'aid in protecting irritated anorectal areas' and provide 'temporary relief of' irritation or burning (21 CFR 346.50). This reflects a formal FDA generally-recognized-as-safe-and-effective (GRASE) determination for symptom relief rather than a recent randomized controlled trial, and the permitted labeling language is limited to protecting/soothing irritated tissue, not resolving hemorrhoids themselves. A separate pharmacology review independently corroborates that witch hazel is, in practice, 'a common ingredient in OTC treatments aimed [at relieving] hemorrhoidal symptoms.' Graded B for the strength and specificity of the regulatory recognition, while noting this is not equivalent to a modern head-to-head efficacy trial.
