claims.useCase: Topical astringent for minor skin irritation, insect bites, and minor cuts
claims.gradeRationale: This is witch hazel's most cited traditional/folk use, and its astringent mechanism (tannins coagulating surface proteins to reduce permeability and mild inflammation) is described in an NCBI Bookshelf pharmacology chapter and echoed by a consumer drug-information monograph, which states witch hazel is applied to the skin to help soothe irritation from small cuts and insect bites. A retrospective observational review of a witch hazel-based scalp product likewise lists insect bites, cracked skin, and minor inflammatory skin conditions among its traditional applications, though this source's author discloses a paid consulting relationship with the product's manufacturer, so it is treated here only as corroborating traditional-use framing, not as independent clinical evidence. However, none of these sources describe a placebo-controlled clinical trial testing witch hazel specifically for cuts or insect bites as a use-case in its own right (the pediatric/eczema/UV-erythema trials that do exist tested other conditions), so this remains a traditional-use claim rather than a graded one. Note that NCCIH, the source used for several other herbs in this app, does not maintain a dedicated fact sheet on witch hazel (its 'Herbs at a Glance' index and a direct nccih.nih.gov/health/witch-hazel URL both return no results), so coverage here relies on NCBI Bookshelf, PMC literature, and consumer drug-information sources instead.

claims.useCase: Mild atopic eczema/dermatitis-related itching, redness, and scaling (topical distillate cream)
claims.gradeRationale: A 14-day, double-blind, randomized trial in 72 patients with moderately severe atopic eczema (Korting et al., 1995, Eur J Clin Pharmacol 48(6):461-5) compared a 5.35% hamamelis distillate cream against its drug-free vehicle and 0.5% hydrocortisone cream. The trial's own PubMed abstract, read directly, resolves what secondary sources describe inconsistently: while all three preparations reduced itching, erythema, and scaling within a week, the hamamelis distillate cream 'did not show a meaningful difference from its drug-free vehicle,' and hydrocortisone was significantly superior to hamamelis on the study's severity criteria. A separate NCBI Bookshelf chapter, citing a different, smaller trial (n=36 atopic dermatitis, n=80 contact dermatitis), reports hamamelis 'slightly superior' to control for inflammation/itching in that trial - but that chapter is itself a secondary source's paraphrase of a still-earlier citation (Brown & Dattner, 1998), one step further removed from the primary data than the directly-read Korting abstract. Graded F per this app's rubric: the larger, better-described, and most directly verifiable trial of this specific use (mild atopic eczema symptom relief) is a controlled RCT that found no meaningful benefit over its own inactive vehicle, even though a low-dose steroid comparator in the same trial did work. This does not mean witch hazel is harmful, only that the best available controlled evidence for this specific use case failed to show a benefit over placebo.

claims.useCase: Acne-related skin inflammation (topical bark extract)
claims.gradeRationale: Evidence here is laboratory/cell-based only, not a human clinical trial. A study exposing cultured human keratinocytes (HaCaT cells) to Cutibacterium acnes or TNF-alpha found a glycolic Hamamelis virginiana bark extract reduced inflammatory markers (IL-6, IL-8) but explicitly reported 'no antibacterial or antibiofilm activities' against C. acnes itself - meaning any plausible benefit would be anti-inflammatory rather than antibacterial. A separate pharmacology review corroborates that acne-related anti-inflammatory activity has been shown in keratinocyte models but does not cite a completed human acne trial. Left ungraded: this is preliminary in vitro evidence, not evidence from people with acne.

safetyNotes.text: The most common topical side effect is dry skin or mild local irritation. Stop use and consult a healthcare provider if skin worsens, does not improve within 7 days, or if bleeding occurs when using a witch hazel product for anorectal irritation.

Allergic/hypersensitivity skin reactions are possible in sensitive individuals. Stop use and seek care promptly if itching, rash, hives, or swelling of the face, lips, mouth, or throat develop after applying witch hazel, as these can be signs of a more serious allergic reaction.

Commercial witch hazel products (astringent 'witch hazel water', toners, wipes) are formulated for external use on intact skin only; product labeling advises against use in deep or open wounds or inserting the product internally (rectally or vaginally) without a healthcare provider's guidance.

Oral/internal ingestion is a different risk profile from common commercial witch hazel water. The steam distillation used to make most commercial witch hazel water removes most of the plant's tannins, whereas bark or leaf decoctions and some internal preparations retain much more tannin. Internal use of tannin-retaining witch hazel preparations has not been well studied for safety in humans, and this report could not find a well-documented case study establishing liver injury or other serious harm from oral witch hazel specifically; in the absence of that evidence, oral use beyond ordinary commercial topical products is not addressed by the FDA's OTC monograph and is generally not recommended without professional guidance.

Little is specifically known about witch hazel's safety in pregnancy or while breastfeeding; consumer drug-information sources state it is not known whether or how witch hazel could affect pregnancy or an unborn baby, or whether it passes into breast milk. Talk to a healthcare provider before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding, especially beyond typical topical/commercial use.

No well-documented drug interactions were identified for topical witch hazel, consistent with its minimal systemic absorption when used on the skin as directed. As with any product, talk to a healthcare provider before use if you take prescription medication or have a chronic skin condition.
